He explains his klība form resulted from a year-long vow of brahmacarya performed at his brother's command. Uttara assumes the role of charioteer, likening the horses to those of Indra and Vāsudeva. Arjuna removes his bangles, binds his hair with white cloth, and strings the gāṇḍīva. The bow’s twang echoes like a falling mountain, shaking the earth and signaling his presence to the Kuru army.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna arms himself and approaches the Kuru army.
chapters.es: Arjuna equips his chariot with the gāṇḍīva bow and summons a divine banner bearing the vānara symbol. As he blows his massive conch shell, the sound causes the horses to kneel and overwhelms Uttara with fear. Arjuna reassures the prince and instructs him to steady the reins. On the opposing side, Droṇa observes ill omens, including the trembling earth and dimming fires, recognizing the distinct sounds of Arjuna's chariot and weaponry as the warrior moves toward the Kuru army.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana prepares for battle and questions his teachers' loyalty.
chapters.es: Duryodhana addresses Bhishma and Drona as a lone warrior approaches the Kuru lines. He asserts that if Arjuna appears before the ajñātavāsa concludes, the Pandavas must return to the forest for twelve years. Suspecting the elders of favoring their former pupil, he dismisses their praise as sentiment. He commands the army to secure the captured godhana and arrange the troops into a defensive vyūha. Rejecting natural omens, he insists that his commanders focus on tactical combat rather than debating the skills of their opponent.

chapters.subtitle: Karna vows to fight Arjuna and protect the Kurus.
chapters.es: Karna observes the panic among the Kuru ranks and vows to stop Arjuna’s advance like a shore halting the sea. He promises to release gold-tufted arrows that swarm like locusts or crawl like snakes toward their target. Invoking the weapons received from Jāmadagnya, he declares his intent to repay his debt to Duryodhana. He aims to strike the monkey from Arjuna’s banner and commands the other soldiers to watch from their chariots as he faces the Pāṇḍava alone.

chapters.subtitle: Kripa warns the Kurus to fight Arjuna together.
chapters.es: Kṛpa rebukes Karṇa for his rashness and disregard for the timing of war. He recounts Arjuna’s previous victories, including the burning of the forest to satisfy Agni and the defeat of the Nivātakavacas. Kṛpa compares facing the Pāṇḍava to grabbing a venomous snake or walking through fire. He warns that Arjuna, now free from thirteen years of exile, resembles a lion released from a trap. He urges the Kuru leaders to stand together in a unified formation to survive the encounter.

chapters.subtitle: Aśvatthāman rebukes Karṇa and warns the Kuru army.
chapters.es: Aśvatthāman rebukes Karṇa for boasting before the cattle are secured or the battle won. He reminds the assembly that the sun and earth perform their duties in silence. He challenges those who won the kingdom with dice to face Arjuna’s arrows. Arjuna approaches to avenge the mistreatment of Draupadī; his bow, gāṇḍīva, now releases sharp metal instead of weighted dice. Acknowledging the bond between teacher and student, Aśvatthāman refuses to engage Arjuna and advises focusing on the Matsya king.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma settles an argument and prepares for battle.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma intervenes to quell the friction between Karṇa and the instructors Droṇa and Kṛpa. He warns that internal dissension, or bheda, destroys an army more surely than any enemy. Duryodhana offers formal apologies, acknowledging the rare combination of brahmāstra and veda within his teachers. With order restored, the leaders turn toward the advancing Arjuna. They debate whether the Pāṇḍava prince has appeared before the end of his exile and organize their ranks to prevent a retreat.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma calculates the exile's end and the army prepares.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma calculates the movement of the kālacakra, accounting for adhikamāsa to confirm that the thirteen-year exile has ended. He asserts that the Pāṇḍavas remain bound by dharma and would not appear prematurely. Duryodhana rejects any peaceful return of the kingdom and orders the army into formation. He divides the troops to secure the captured cattle while Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Karṇa take their stations. Duryodhana assumes the rear position, readying the Kaurava forces to face Arjuna in battle.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna attacks the Kuru army and retrieves the cattle.
chapters.es: Arjuna enters the battlefield, his arrival signaled by the thunderous sound of the gāṇḍīva bow and the monkey banner. He shoots two arrows to salute Droṇa’s feet and two more to brush past his ears as a greeting. Ignoring the gathered commanders, he commands his charioteer to pursue Duryodhana directly. After Arjuna rains arrows upon the soldiers and sounds his conch, the stolen cattle take fright at the noise and stampede back toward the south.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna defeats Kuru heroes and forces Karṇa to flee.
chapters.es: Arjuna directs Uttara to drive his white horses into the Kuru ranks. He aims for Duryodhana but encounters a surge of chariot-warriors. Using the Gāṇḍīva, he destroys Vikarṇa’s banner and kills Śatruṃtapa. The battlefield fills with fallen men clad in gold and iron armor. After Arjuna decapitates Saṅgrāmajit, Karṇa retaliates with a heavy volley. Arjuna responds by piercing Karṇa’s limbs and neck with arrows. Wounded and unable to endure the assault, Karṇa abandons the front line and flees the field.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna identifies the Kuru commanders and orders an attack.
chapters.es: After Karna retreats, the Kuru princes launch a coordinated attack. Arjuna instructs Uttara to guide the chariot through the ranks, identifying each commander by their distinct standards. He points out Kripa by his blue banner and Drona by his golden kamaṇḍalu. Following custom, Arjuna resolves to circle Drona with respect before engaging. He marks Duryodhana’s elephant flag and Karna’s standard for direct confrontation. Finally, he sights Bhishma’s five-star banner and golden armor, ordering Uttara to steer toward Kripa to begin the counter-offensive.

chapters.subtitle: Gods and kings gather to watch the upcoming battle.
chapters.es: The Kuru armies gather like slow clouds at summer’s end, with horses and elephants positioned for combat. Indra arrives on his chariot, followed by the Maruts and the thirty-three gods. Ancient kings like Yayāti and Sagara take their seats in golden vimāna vehicles to witness the duel between Arjuna and Bhīṣma. Divine garlands scent the air as red banners and umbrellas fill the sky. The dust settles and a breeze blows while the celestials watch the human warriors prepare their weapons for battle.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna defeats Kṛpa in a chariot duel.
chapters.es: Arjuna and Kṛpa engage in a swift exchange of arrows. From the gāṇḍīva, Arjuna releases shafts that darken the sky, while Kṛpa counters with precise strikes. Arjuna kills Kṛpa’s four horses and shatters multiple bows as his opponent attempts to recover. Though he destroys Kṛpa's chariot, driver, and flag, Arjuna spares his life out of respect. After Arjuna deflects a thrown spear and a heavy gadā, other Kuru warriors rush in to carry the defeated and weaponless Kṛpa away from the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna battles his teacher Drona on the battlefield.
chapters.es: Arjuna identifies Drona’s chariot by its golden vedī banner and commands Uttara to approach. After a polite greeting, the archer engages his former teacher. Their arrows fill the sky, blocking the sun and creating a sound like crackling bamboo. Arjuna neutralizes Drona’s aindra and vāyavya weapons with his own. Displaying rapid fire from the gāṇḍīva bow, he shatters Drona’s armor and standard. Ashvatthama rushes forward to protect his father, providing Drona an opening to retreat from the intense exchange of fire.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna fights Aśvatthāman and then challenges Karṇa
chapters.es: Arjuna intercepts Aśvatthāman’s assault, filling the sky with arrows that obscure the sun. The clashing weapons sound like burning bamboo. Aśvatthāman severs the bowstring with a kṣura blade, but Arjuna quickly re-strings the Gāṇḍīva. While Aśvatthāman’s arrows deplete, Arjuna’s celestial quivers remain full. When Karṇa enters the fray and draws his bow, Arjuna turns his attention away from Aśvatthāman to confront his rival. With eyes red from anger, he advances to engage Karṇa in single combat.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna defeats Karna in a chariot duel.
chapters.es: Arjuna challenges Karna, recalling the insults directed at Draupādī in the royal assembly. He mocks Karna’s previous flight and the death of his brother. Karna defends his earlier actions, accusing Arjuna of breaking the forest exile early. In the ensuing duel, Arjuna uses the gāṇḍīva to shatter Karna’s bow and kill his horses. A final arrow pierces Karna’s chest, causing him to lose consciousness. Overwhelmed by pain, Karna retreats from the fight while Arjuna and Uttara shout in victory.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna defeats several Kuru princes while moving toward Bhīṣma.
chapters.es: Arjuna instructs Uttara to steer the chariot toward Bhīṣma’s golden palm tree standard. Recalling his victories over demons and the celestial weapons received from Indra and Rudra, he prepares to strike. He vows to fell the Kuru army like a forest. Duḥśāsana and Vikarṇa intercept him, but Arjuna shatters their bows and strikes them with heavy arrows. He kills the horses of Duḥsaha and Viviṃśati, forcing the princes to flee as he clears the path through the opposing ranks.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna defeats the Kaurava army in battle.
chapters.es: Arjuna faces the combined Kaurava force, pinning them down with arrows that pierce iron armor. He moves with such speed that drawing and releasing his bow, Gāṇḍīva, appears as a single motion. Severed heads wearing earrings and limbs adorned with bracelets cover the earth. Arjuna releases his long-held anger, creating a river of blood where bones act as moss and chariots serve as islands. The army retreats as he shines like the midday sun, scattering the remaining warriors from their horses and chariots.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna uses divine weapons to defeat the Kuru army.
chapters.es: Duryodhana, Karṇa, Droṇa, and the Kuru leaders surround Arjuna, whose chariot bears a monkey flag. They rain arrows like monsoon clouds until no space remains on his vehicle. Arjuna laughs and invokes the aindra weapon on his gāṇḍīva bow. His counter-arrows spread like sunbeams, covering the entire Kuru force. The bow flashes like lightning across ten directions, resembling Indra’s rainbow. Faced with this barrage, the Kuru warriors lose heart and flee the battlefield, abandoning their positions to save their lives.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna and Bhishma fight a duel with divine weapons.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma advances under a white umbrella, blowing his conch to challenge Arjuna. He strikes the monkey emblem on Arjuna’s banner with eight arrows. Arjuna retaliates, shearing away Bhīṣma's umbrella and severing his bow. Both warriors discharge celestial weapons—the āgneya and vāyavya—as deities watch from the sky. Arjuna’s gāṇḍīva forms a circle of fire, releasing arrows that resemble rows of swans. After Arjuna pierces Bhīṣma’s chest with ten shafts, the wounded warrior loses consciousness and his charioteer drives him away.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna defeats Vikarna’s elephant and Duryodhana retreats.
chapters.es: Duryodhana confronts Arjuna and strikes his forehead with a bhalla arrow. Blood flows down Arjuna’s face like a golden garland. Arjuna retaliates by piercing Duryodhana’s chest and striking the massive elephant of Vikarna. The beast collapses like a mountain hit by a thunderbolt, forcing Vikarna to flee to another chariot. As the Kuru forces break, Duryodhana turns his chariot from the fight. Arjuna follows, shouting taunts that mock the king for abandoning his name and duty while fleeing the field.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna uses a weapon to reclaim the stolen cattle.
chapters.es: Arjuna faces the Kuru army as they rally around Duryodhana. He discharges the sammohanam weapon, plunging the warriors into a deep trance. Following Arjuna's instructions, Prince Uttara descends to collect the garments of the unconscious leaders. As the Kurus awaken, Bhishma credits Arjuna’s restraint for sparing their lives. Arjuna fires arrows in salutation to his preceptors and shoots the crown from Duryodhana's head. With the stolen cattle recovered, the Kuru forces retreat while Arjuna and Uttara turn back toward the city.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna recovers the cattle and spares the defeated soldiers.
chapters.es: Arjuna defeats the Kuru forces and recovers the stolen cattle. Straggling soldiers emerge from the forest with disheveled hair and folded hands. Although they are exhausted by hunger and thirst, Arjuna grants them safety, refusing to strike those in distress. He tells Uttara to water the horses and gather the herdsmen for the return journey. Following Arjuna’s instructions, Uttara sends messengers to the city of Virāṭa to proclaim the victory in the prince's own name.

chapters.subtitle: King Virāṭa strikes Kaṅka during a dice game.
chapters.es: King Virāṭa returns from battle and orders citywide celebrations upon hearing messengers announce Prince Uttara’s victory. While playing akṣa, the king boasts of his son’s skill, but Kaṅka attributes the success to the charioteer Bṛhannaḍā. Enraged, Virāṭa strikes Kaṅka with a game piece, drawing blood from his nose. Sairandhrī quickly catches the blood in a golden bowl. When Uttara arrives, Kaṅka warns the guard to admit the prince alone, fearing Bṛhannaḍā might kill the king upon seeing the injury.

chapters.subtitle: Uttara reveals that a divine youth won the battle.
chapters.es: Prince Uttara enters the court and finds Yudhiṣṭhira bleeding from the king’s blow. He warns Virāṭa of the peril in striking a Brāhmaṇa, leading the king to ask for forgiveness. When Virāṭa credits his son for the victory over the Kuru army, Uttara reveals that a divine youth won the battle. He describes how this warrior defeated Bhīṣma and Karṇa to reclaim the stolen cattle. Bṛhannaḍā gives the captured garments to Princess Uttarā while Arjuna secretly coordinates with Yudhiṣṭhira to end their year of concealment.

chapters.subtitle: The Pandavas reveal their identity to King Virata.
chapters.es: After completing their year of concealment, the five Pāṇḍava brothers bathe and dress in white garments. They enter King Virāṭa's court and occupy the royal seats. When the king questions why his former companion, Kaṅka, sits upon a throne, Arjuna reveals the true identity of the eldest brother. He recounts Yudhiṣṭhira’s history of sovereign rule, his protection of the vulnerable, and his performance of sacrifices. Arjuna asserts that this son of Kuntī, who formerly commanded thousands of chariots, deserves any earthly seat.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna reveals the Pandavas' true identities to King Virāta.
chapters.es: Arjuna identifies his brothers and Draupadī to King Virāta. He names Bhīma as the cook who killed the Kīcakas, and Nakula and Sahadeva as the keepers of horses and cows. Prince Uttara describes Arjuna’s defeat of the Kuru army and the recovery of the cattle. Acknowledging their protection, Virāta offers his entire kingdom and wealth to Yudhiṣṭhira. To formalize their bond, the king offers his daughter Uttarā to Arjuna, who accepts her as a daughter-in-law to unite their families.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna’s son Abhimanyu marries King Virāṭa’s daughter Uttarā.
chapters.es: Arjuna declines King Virāṭa's offer to marry Uttarā, citing their father-daughter bond formed during his year as her dance teacher. He requests her instead as a bride for his son Abhimanyu. The Pāṇḍavas relocate to Upaplavya, where Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, and the Vṛṣṇis arrive with the groom. Drupada and other allies assemble their armies. The wedding concludes with music, feasts, and gifts. Yudhiṣṭhira accepts Uttarā as his snuṣā, distributing gold, cattle, and textiles to the brāhmaṇas as the city celebrates.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna proposes sending a messenger to the Kauravas.
chapters.es: Following Abhimanyu’s wedding, kings assemble in Virāṭa’s gem-encrusted sabhā. Kṛṣṇa addresses the gathered monarchs, including Drupada and the Pāṇḍavas, to recount the unfair dice game and the completion of the thirteen-year exile. He proposes a diplomatic path, emphasizing Yudhiṣṭhira’s preference for dharma over ill-gotten power. Kṛṣṇa suggests sending a virtuous envoy to the Kurus to negotiate the peaceful return of the kingdom. Balarāma supports this call for a diplomatic settlement to avoid immediate conflict.

chapters.subtitle: Balarāma proposes peace while blaming Yudhiṣṭhira for the gambling.
chapters.es: Balarāma addresses the kings, advocating for a peaceful division of the kingdom. He suggests an envoy visit Dhṛtarāṣṭra's court to negotiate using sāma. Recounting the game of dice, he identifies Yudhiṣṭhira’s choice to play against Śakuni as the reason for his exile. He urges the messenger to adopt a humble tone to secure the Pāṇḍavas’ interests. Sātyaki interrupts the speech, rising in anger to denounce Balarāma's conciliatory approach and his defense of the Kurus.

chapters.subtitle: Satyaki argues for reclaiming the kingdom through force.
chapters.es: Satyaki rejects conciliatory pleas and rebukes those who find fault in Yudhishthira. He identifies the Kauravas as deceitful gamblers who seized the kingdom through trickery rather than dharma. Vowing to strike down the sons of Dhritarashtra with sharp arrows, he asserts that the Pandavas must reclaim their ancestral land by force. He names Arjuna and Bhima as an unstoppable force, arguing that killing ātatāyinaḥ, or dangerous aggressors, is a righteous act far superior to begging for mercy from enemies.

chapters.subtitle: The Pandavas gather allies and send a messenger.
chapters.es: Sātyaki rejects the proposal for soft speech, arguing that Duryodhana perceives gentleness as weakness. He advises the Pāṇḍavas to summon their allies immediately, reaching out to kings like Śalya and Bhagadatta before the Kurus can secure their loyalty. He lists leaders from the Śakas and Kāmbojas to be mobilized across the land. Simultaneously, he suggests sending a family purohita to the court of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to present their terms, ensuring the army prepares even as diplomacy begins.

chapters.subtitle: Kings prepare for war and Drupada sends a messenger.
chapters.es: Following the marriage celebrations, the kings acknowledge Drupada’s age and wisdom, asking him to initiate negotiations. Kṛṣṇa departs for Dvārakā while Yudhiṣṭhira and Virāṭa organize their military forces. Messengers travel to distant lands to recruit allies, and rulers arrive with their divisions, shaking the earth with their movement. Simultaneously, Duryodhana gathers his own supporters. To seek a peaceful settlement, Drupada dispatches his learned purohita to the Kuru capital with a message approved by the Pāṇḍavas.

chapters.subtitle: Drupada sends a priest to negotiate for the Pāṇḍavas.
chapters.es: King Drupada appoints his learned purohita to travel to Hastināpura as a formal envoy. He instructs the priest to remind Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the deception used against Yudhiṣṭhira and to recount the family's ancient dharma. The mission aims to create internal division among warriors like Bhīṣma and Droṇa, buying time for the Pāṇḍavas to gather their armies. Relying on his status as a brāhmaṇa, the priest sets out during a puṣya alignment to demand the restoration of the Pāṇḍava kingdom.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna and Duryodhana ask Krishna for help in war.
chapters.es: Duryodhana and Arjuna arrive in Dvārakā to seek Kṛṣṇa’s support. Duryodhana sits at the head of the sleeping Kṛṣṇa, while Arjuna stands at his feet with palms joined. Waking, Kṛṣṇa offers a choice between his nārāyaṇa army and his unarmed self. Arjuna chooses the non-combatant Kṛṣṇa, leaving the troops to Duryodhana. Balarāma refuses to fight for either side, and Kṛtavarman pledges an army to the Kauravas. Finally, Kṛṣṇa agrees to serve as Arjuna’s charioteer, fulfilling the warrior's request.

chapters.subtitle: Shalya joins Duryodhana and promises Yudhishthira a secret favor.
chapters.es: Shalya leads a massive army toward the Pandavas, but Duryodhana intercepts him with lavish rest-houses. Deceived by this hospitality, Shalya grants Duryodhana a boon and agrees to join his side. Shalya then travels to Upaplavya to inform Yudhishthira of his pact. Yudhishthira requests that Shalya serve as the charioteer for Karna and demoralize the warrior during battle. Shalya promises to discourage the sūtaputra and consoles the brothers by comparing their exile to the hardships faced by Indra.

chapters.subtitle: Indra kills Triśiras and faces the demon Vṛtra.
chapters.es: Tvaṣṭṛ creates the three-headed Triśiras, whose intense tapas alarms Indra. After celestial nymphs fail to distract the ascetic, Indra strikes him with a vajra. At Indra's command, a woodcutter severs the heads, and birds called kapiñjala, tittira, and kalaviṅka fly from the neck. Enraged, Tvaṣṭṛ conjures the demon Vṛtra from fire. Vṛtra swallows Indra in combat, but a divinely induced yawn forces him to release the god. Facing Vṛtra's growing power, the gods retreat to seek counsel from Viṣṇu.

chapters.subtitle: Indra kills Vṛtra and flees due to his sin.
chapters.es: Indra and the gods seek Viṣṇu’s aid against the world-consuming Vṛtra. Following Viṣṇu’s counsel, sages negotiate a peace treaty. Vṛtra demands immunity from all weapons, dry or wet materials, and death during day or night. At twilight by the ocean, Indra strikes Vṛtra with phena entered by Viṣṇu. Though victorious, the sin of brahmahatyā drives Indra into hiding within the waters. The earth withers as the throne of heaven falls vacant, causing a global drought and chaos among all beings.

chapters.subtitle: Nahuṣa becomes king of heaven and pursues Indra’s wife.
chapters.es: The gods and ṛṣis crown Nahuṣa as king of heaven to replace the missing Indra. They grant him a boon to drain the tejas of any being he observes. Abandoning his duties, Nahuṣa seeks pleasure in the gardens of Nandana and atop mount Kailāsa. He demands that Indra’s queen, Śacī, submit to him as her new lord. Śacī flees to the priest Bṛhaspati, who promises that Indra will return to reclaim her. This defiance fuels the new king's anger.

chapters.subtitle: Nahuṣa demands Indra's wife while Bṛhaspati protects her.
chapters.es: Nahuṣa demands Śacī, the wife of Indra, as his own. When the gods and sages advise him to rule righteously, he justifies his lust by citing Indra’s past sins. Fearing Nahuṣa's power, the gods ask Bṛhaspati to surrender her. Bṛhaspati refuses to betray a refugee, quoting ancient verses on the ruin that follows such treachery. At his suggestion, Śacī asks Nahuṣa for a delay. She visits the king, who welcomes her with lust, unaware of the gods' plan for his downfall.

chapters.subtitle: Indra is purified by sacrifice and Śacī seeks him.
chapters.es: Nahuṣa demands that Indrāṇī accept him as her husband. She requests a delay to search for Indra, who remains in hiding. Following Viṣṇu’s counsel, the gods perform an aśvamedha to cleanse Indra of brahmahatyā. He distributes this sin among trees, rivers, mountains, the earth, and women. Although purified, Indra stays concealed to avoid Nahuṣa's strength. Indrāṇī then invokes the deity Upaśruti and prays for a vision that will reveal her husband’s secret location.

chapters.subtitle: Indrāṇī finds Indra hiding and asks for his help.
chapters.es: Indrāṇī follows the goddess Upasṛti across the Himavat mountains to a remote lake. They enter a lotus stalk to find Indra hiding within a thin bisatantu fiber in a minute form. After reciting his past deeds, Indrāṇī describes the tyranny of Nahuṣa, who has seized the heavens and demanded her hand. She pleads with her husband to cast off his disguise, reclaim his divine strength, and slay the usurper to save her from his advances.

chapters.subtitle: Nahusha forces sages to carry him while Indra hides.
chapters.es: Indra instructs Śacī to demand that Nahuṣa visit her in a vehicle never before used by gods or demons. Driven by pride, Nahuṣa compels the saptarṣis to carry his palanquin. While Nahuṣa exploits the sages, Bṛhaspati performs a ritual to find the hidden Indra. He commands Agni to search the mountains, forests, and sky. When Agni hesitates at the ocean's edge, Bṛhaspati reminds him that fire can enter the water as its own place of origin.

chapters.subtitle: Agni finds Indra, who prepares to reclaim his throne.
chapters.es: Bṛhaspati praises Agni, who searches the waters and finds Indra hiding inside a lotus stalk. Having shrunk to the size of an atom, Indra regains his strength through the hymns of the gods. He learns that Nahuṣa has usurped the throne and terrifies the heavens with a poisonous gaze. Indra assembles Kubera, Yama, Varuṇa, and Agni, promising them bhāga—sacrificial portions—and specific authorities over wealth, ancestors, and waters to secure their alliance against the mortal king.

chapters.subtitle: Agastya curses Nahuṣa to become a serpent on earth.
chapters.es: Agastya visits Indra to explain the fall of Nahuṣa. While sages carried the king's litter, Nahuṣa dismissed the authority of Vedic mantra terms concerning cattle. His arrogance culminated in kicking Agastya's head. The sage cursed Nahuṣa for treating brahmarṣis as draft animals and disregarding sacred law. Stripped of his merit, Nahuṣa falls to the earth to dwell as a serpent for ten thousand years. Indra regains his throne as devarāja while gods, gandharvas, and personified rivers celebrate his return.

chapters.subtitle: Indra regains his throne and Śalya promises his help.
chapters.es: Surrounded by the gods, Indra mounts his elephant Airāvata and returns to rule the three worlds with his queen, Indrāṇī. He honors the sage Aṅgiras, naming a Veda after him and granting his hymns a share in the yajña. Śalya uses this account to comfort Yudhiṣṭhira, predicting the downfall of the Kauravas. Before departing for the enemy camp, Śalya agrees to demoralize Karṇa while acting as his charioteer. Listening to this victory brings success and long life to kings about to enter battle.

chapters.subtitle: Kings bring their armies to the Pandavas and Kauravas.
chapters.es: Satyaki leads an akṣauhiṇī of soldiers armed with paraśu and tomara to join Yudhishthira. Dhrishtaketu, Jayatsena, and the Pandya king arrive with their forces, while Drupada and Virata bring mountain warriors. These seven divisions gather for the Pandavas. Conversely, Bhagadatta brings Kirāta troops to Duryodhana, followed by Shalya, Kritavarma, and Sudakshina’s western allies. Eleven divisions eventually crowd the Kaurava territories, overflowing Hastinapura into the Kurujāṅgala and the banks of the Ganga. Drupada’s envoy observes this mobilization.

chapters.subtitle: Drupada's priest asks the Kuru court for land.
chapters.es: Drupada's priest enters the Kuru assembly and speaks to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, and Vidura. He identifies the Pāṇḍavas’ right to their father’s wealth and lists the hardships of their thirteen-year exile and the deception in the gambling hall. Although the Pāṇḍavas seek a peaceful settlement (sāma), the priest cautions the court about their military strength. He mentions seven akṣauhiṇīs and the combined force of Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, urging the Kurus to return the kingdom before conflict begins.

chapters.subtitle: The Kuru court debates peace and sends Sañjaya.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma acknowledges the Pāṇḍava claim to their inheritance and praises the martial skill of Arjuna. He urges peace, noting the difficulty of facing them in battle. Karṇa interrupts, dismissing the messenger’s claims and insisting that Yudhiṣṭhira must abide by the terms of the gambling wager. He asserts that Duryodhana will not yield land out of fear. After Bhīṣma reminds Karṇa of his defeat at Virāṭa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra intervenes. He decides to send Sañjaya to the Pāṇḍava camp to negotiate.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra sends Sanjaya to the Pandavas to seek peace.
chapters.es: Dhṛtarāṣṭra commands Sañjaya to travel to Upaplavya to greet the Pāṇḍavas. He recounts the military alliances supporting Yudhiṣṭhira, noting the strength of Bhīma and the archer Arjuna. Fearing the combined power of the Gāṇḍīva bow and Kṛṣṇa’s counsel, the king admits his sons' vulnerability despite their greed. He lists the kings gathering for battle, including the Cedis and Pāṇḍyas. Finally, he instructs Sañjaya to offer words of peace, hoping to quell Yudhiṣṭhira’s anger before it destroys the Kurus.

chapters.subtitle: Sañjaya meets Yudhiṣṭhira and conveys greetings from the Kurus.
chapters.es: Sañjaya arrives at Upaplavya to meet the Pāṇḍavas. Yudhiṣṭhira receives the envoy and inquires about the well-being of the Kuru elders, including Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra. He asks whether the court still respects the traditional rights of brāhmaṇas and the livelihood of his own dependents. Recalling his brothers' past victories, he reminds Sañjaya of Arjuna’s Gāṇḍīva bow and Bhīma’s strength, questioning if the Kurus remember the time the Pāṇḍavas rescued them from enemies at Dvaitavana.

chapters.subtitle: Sañjaya asks Yudhiṣṭhira to seek peace with the Kurus.
chapters.es: Sañjaya reports on the Kuru elders and the blind king's sorrow. He describes how the court remembers Arjuna’s archery and Bhīmasena’s mace. Despite the Pāṇḍavas’ past suffering, Sañjaya urges Yudhiṣṭhira to rely on prajñā to establish śama between the warring families. He warns against the sin of mitradroha and acknowledges that the righteous should not abandon their nature for wealth. Sañjaya then prepares to deliver the specific message sent by Dhṛtarāṣṭra to ensure the welfare of all kings gathered.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya delivers a message of peace to the Pandavas.
chapters.es: Sañjaya enters the assembly and conveys King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s desire for peace. He commends the Pāṇḍavas for their integrity, likening a potential fault in their conduct to a dark añjanabindu on a white garment. Warning that war results in total destruction, he asserts that victory through the slaughter of kinsmen is indistinguishable from defeat. He acknowledges the formidable strength of both armies. Finally, with folded hands, he appeals to Vāsudeva and Arjuna to avoid conflict and ensure the survival of the Kuru and Sṛñjaya lineages.

chapters.subtitle: Yudhiṣṭhira offers peace if his kingdom is returned.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira asserts that peace is better than war, though human desire grows like a fire fed by sarpiṣ. He notes that King Dhṛtarāṣṭra ignores the wise Vidura, favoring the counsel of Duryodhana and Karṇa instead. Likening the king’s actions to lighting a forest fire and then seeking shade, Yudhiṣṭhira warns that no enemy can withstand Bhīmasena or the bow gāṇḍīva. He offers to end the hostility if the king restores the Pāṇḍava kingdom at Indraprastha.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya tells Yudhiṣṭhira to avoid war and choose peace.
chapters.es: Sanjaya urges Yudhiṣṭhira to choose a life of begging over the slaughter of kinsmen. He describes life as a transient flow and warns that even a kingdom bounded by oceans cannot avert death. Recalling Yudhiṣṭhira’s history of yajña and Vedic study, Sanjaya argues that the fruits of karma follow the doer. He identifies anger as a disease of the head and pleads with the prince to spare elders like Bhīṣma and Droṇa to preserve his path of dharma.

chapters.subtitle: Yudhishthira discusses duty in distress and seeks Krishna's advice.
chapters.es: Yudhishthira distinguishes between steady duty and āpaddharma, the conduct required during times of distress. He argues that actions appearing as adharma may be righteous when the natural order fails. Declaring he seeks no kingdom or celestial realm through injustice, he defers the choice of war or peace to Krishna. He describes Krishna as a leader of the vṛṣṇi and andhaka clans who provides for his people like rain after heat. Yudhishthira commits to following Krishna’s judgment and nīti without hesitation.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna explains the duty of action and seeks peace.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa tells Sañjaya that the world functions through unwearied karma, citing the tireless movements of the sun, wind, and rivers. He defines the duties of each varṇa, justifying war when land is stolen. After recalling the humiliation of Draupadī, he describes Yudhiṣṭhira and Duryodhana as opposing trees of dharma and wrath. Likening the Pāṇḍavas to tigers in the Kuru forest, he resolves to visit the court himself to seek peace before the brothers resort to weapons.

chapters.subtitle: Yudhiṣṭhira sends greetings and an ultimatum to the Kurus.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira grants Sañjaya leave to depart for Hastināpura, praising the envoy’s gentle speech. He entrusts Sañjaya with greetings for the entire Kuru household, from the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the warrior Bhīṣma to the preceptor Droṇa. He inquires after the welfare of his cousins, the women in the inner apartments, and the common laborers. His message extends to the blind, the orphaned, and the disabled. Finally, Yudhiṣṭhira demands the return of Śakrapura or a trial by combat, grounding his resolve in dharma.

chapters.subtitle: Yudhiṣṭhira asks for five villages to prevent war.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira sends Sañjaya to the Kuru court with a final offer of peace. He acknowledges the power of fate and asks Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, and Vidura to protect the family line. Reminding Duryodhana of the humiliations endured in the assembly and during exile, he demands their share of the kingdom. To prevent the slaughter of kinsmen, he requests only five villages: Kuśasthala, Vṛkasthala, Āsandī, Vāraṇāvata, and one other. He declares himself ready for either gentle peace or harsh war to uphold dharma.

chapters.subtitle: Sañjaya returns to the palace and criticizes the king.
chapters.es: Sañjaya returns to Hāstinapura and enters the inner palace to meet Dhṛtarāṣṭra. After conveying greetings from Yudhiṣṭhira, he speaks bluntly about the king’s failings. He likens Yudhiṣṭhira shedding sin to a snake casting off its old skin. Sañjaya warns that the king’s submission to his sons’ greed ensures the destruction of the Kurus. He compares human action to a wooden puppet moved by higher forces. Finally, exhausted by the journey, Sañjaya retires, deferring the public message for the morning assembly.

chapters.subtitle: Vidura gives moral advice to the restless King Dhritarashtra.
chapters.es: Anxious over a messenger’s return, a restless king summons his brother for counsel. The advisor identifies sleeplessness as the burden of the fearful or the thief, then details the conduct of a paṇḍita. He categorizes human failings into numbered groups, warning against the six vices of nidrā, tandrī, bhaya, krodha, ālasya, and dīrghasūtratā. Describing the body as a nine-gated house, he urges the king to renounce greed and restore the sons of Pandu to their rightful status.

chapters.subtitle: A counselor advises the king on leadership and self-control.
chapters.es: A counselor advises an anxious king to govern through self-restraint and steady dharma. He warns that greed acts like a baited hook or a charcoal burner destroying a forest for profit. A ruler must instead collect wealth like a bee gathering nectar. The body serves as a chariot where the intellect reins in the unruly horses of the senses. While arrows can be removed from flesh, harsh speech leaves permanent wounds. To save the state, the king must favor the patient Yudhiṣṭhira.

chapters.subtitle: Prahlada judges his son and Vidura lists human virtues.
chapters.es: Virochana and Sudhanvan wager their lives over their own merit. Prahlada decides between his son and the truth, declaring the Brahman superior to the Asura. Sudhanvan spares the prince but requires him to wash the Brahman's feet in a maiden's presence. This example of ārjava precedes a list of eight human qualities, including prajñā and dama. The text warns against lying for land and concludes by advising against placing authority in the hands of the cruel while urging the protection of the Pandavas.

chapters.subtitle: Proper conduct and family unity lead to peace.
chapters.es: A sage appearing as a swan instructs the Sādhya deities to avoid rūkṣā vāc, or harsh speech, which burns like fire. He ranks righteous speech as the highest of four levels, above truth and pleasantry. Family status depends on vṛtta rather than wealth. Just as a forest of trees withstands a storm while a lone tree falls, united kinsmen remain secure. A ruler must swallow his manyu like a bitter medicine to reconcile cousins and preserve the lineage.

chapters.subtitle: Advice on royal conduct, wisdom, and family protection.
chapters.es: Foolish men strike the air or try to bend unbendable bows. Five types of bala sustain a leader, but prajñā is the superior strength, surpassing physical force and wealth. Kinsmen act as tigers in a forest, safe only while they protect one another. A leader sacrifices an individual for a family or a village for a kingdom, and values those who speak unpleasant but beneficial truths. These principles of dharma ensure a full lifespan and royal success.

chapters.subtitle: Proper social conduct and principles of royal leadership
chapters.es: A person rises to greet elders to regain their prāṇa. Guests receive a seat, water for washing feet, and food, though specific sinners remain excluded from hospitality. Domestic duties involve placing mothers in kitchens and fathers in inner chambers while the leader personally tends to agriculture. Royal counsel thrives in secluded forests or mountaintops to ensure secrecy. The earth belongs to those who control their anger and share wealth with servants. A state led by gamblers or children sinks like a stone raft in a river.

chapters.subtitle: Practical rules for family loyalty and moral behavior.
chapters.es: A person moves like a wooden puppet pulled by strings, governed by higher forces. Prosperity grows when one supports suffering jñāti and shares food and conversation with kin. Neglecting family brings future regret, just as an arrow-struck deer suffers. Strength lies in kṣamā, or forgiveness, and conquering krodha with its opposite. One must not do to others what is disagreeable to oneself. Ending the conflict requires treating all children with samatā, ensuring the family remains unsunk in the depths of ruin.

chapters.subtitle: Vidura gives moral advice and the king blames fate.
chapters.es: A person should shed ill-gotten wealth like a snake discards its skin. Truth serves as the water in the river of the soul, while self-control forms the banks. When a body reaches the funeral pyre, kin and riches depart, leaving only karma to accompany the dead. After defining the duties of the four varṇa, Vidura urges the return of the Pāṇḍavas. Dhṛtarāṣṭra acknowledges these truths but claims fate overrules his will, remaining tethered to his sons.

chapters.subtitle: Vidura summons Sanatsujata to instruct King Dhritarashtra.
chapters.es: Dhritarashtra asks for further knowledge, prompting Vidura to mention the sage Sanatsujata’s claim that mṛtyu does not exist. Because his birth from a śūdra womb prevents him from speaking on secret matters, Vidura meditates upon the sage, who then appears in the hall. Vidura welcomes him and asks him to instruct the king. He seeks a path for the king to transcend dualities like priya and dveṣya and the physical constraints of hunger, fear, and age.

chapters.subtitle: Heedlessness causes death while knowledge leads to immortality.
chapters.es: Pramāda, or heedlessness, is the only true death, while apramāda leads to immortality. Death does not prowl like a tiger; it arises within the body as anger and desire. Those who pursue sensory objects fall into the darkness of repeated birth. A seeker uses jñāna to strike down rising desires. Honor and mauna cannot coexist, so the wise live unnoticed. Six qualities—truth, honesty, modesty, self-control, purity, and knowledge—provide the path to overcoming the internal reach of death.

chapters.subtitle: Sanatsujata defines a true scholar through conduct and truth.
chapters.es: Sanatsujata explains that reciting ṛc, yajus, and sāman verses cannot protect a person from the consequences of their actions. Like birds leaving a nest, the chandāṃsi abandon the deceitful at death. A seeker must avoid twelve vices, including anger and greed, which stalk humans like hunters. One practices dama by overcoming eighteen faults and following twelve mahāvrata vows. Knowing the Vedas is distinct from knowing the vedya, the truth found through satya and silence.

chapters.subtitle: Attaining Brahman through the four stages of studenthood.
chapters.es: The practice of brahmacarya unfolds in four stages of service to the ācārya. A seeker extracts the self from the body like a fiber pulled from muñja grass. While parents provide a physical frame, the teacher grants a second, immortal birth. This discipline requires the surrender of pride and wealth. The resulting knowledge reveals brahman, an eternal state beyond the colors of the sky or the verses of the Vedas. It exists as a reality subtler than a razor’s edge yet larger than the mountains.

chapters.subtitle: The eternal spirit lives in the heart of everyone.
chapters.es: A great light shines where the sun draws its brilliance and gods offer worship. This source sustains the earth, sky, and oceans. In the heart, a thumb-sized puruṣa resides, unseen by eyes but grasped through the mind. Like a bee collecting honey or birds landing on a golden aśvattha tree, the seeker finds the one who swallows the sun and moon. This being is the father, mother, and son of all, remaining complete even when fullness is taken from it.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya returns and greets the Kuru assembly.
chapters.es: At daybreak, kings and warriors gather in a hall paved with gold and ivory. Dhṛtarāṣṭra enters with elders like Bhīṣma and Droṇa, followed by Duryodhana and his brothers. They take seats of gold and stone, filling the space like lions in a mountain cave. A gatekeeper announces the messenger's arrival. Sañjaya descends from his chariot and enters the assembly. He delivers the formal greetings of the Pāṇḍava brothers, addressing each relative and ally according to their rank and age.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna warns Duryodhana of the coming war's destruction.
chapters.es: Arjuna stands beside Keśava and issues a final warning to the Kuru court. He describes Bhīma wielding a mace and Śikhaṇḍin advancing toward Bhīṣma. Invoking the past deeds of Vāsudeva, such as the slaying of Naraka and Mura, he declares that Kṛṣṇa’s presence as his driver ensures Kuru defeat. Arjuna reports that his bow, Gāṇḍīva, vibrates and his arrows leap from their quivers. If the kingdom is not restored, he will consume the opposing army like fire in a summer forest.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma identifies Krishna and Arjuna as ancient divine warriors
chapters.es: Bhīṣma explains how the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa once appeared before Brahmā to defend the gods from Asura tribes. He identifies Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna as these same ancient warriors, citing Arjuna’s victories over the Nivātakavaca and Kālakhañja demons. When Karṇa boasts of his strength, Bhīṣma recalls Karṇa’s failures at Virāṭa and the Ghoṣayātrā. Despite warnings from Bhīṣma and Droṇa about the pair's divine nature, Dhṛtarāṣṭra ignores their advice and questions Sañjaya about Arjuna’s intentions.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya names the many warriors allied with the Pandavas.
chapters.es: Dhṛtarāṣṭra questions Sañjaya about the allies gathered around Yudhiṣṭhira. Overwhelmed by the memory of the Pāṇḍava forces, Sañjaya collapses in the assembly. Upon regaining consciousness, he enumerates the warriors prepared for battle. He describes Bhīma’s physical power and Arjuna’s alliance with Vāsudeva. He lists the supporting kings, including Drupada, Virāṭa, and Dhṛṣṭaketu. The account details the presence of Śikhaṇḍin, the five Kekaya brothers, and the youthful Abhimanyu, all standing armed alongside the Matsya and Kāśī kings.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra fears Bhima’s strength and his golden mace.
chapters.es: Dhritarashtra spends sleepless nights sighing with fear as he anticipates the arrival of Bhimasena on the battlefield. He describes Bhima as a tiger among cattle, taller than Arjuna by a prādeśa, wielding an iron gadā that resembles the brahmadaṇḍa. Recalling the death of Jarasandha, the king laments that his sons ignored Vidura’s warnings. He foresees Bhima crushing the heads of elephants and breaking the Kaurava ranks like a forest fire fanned by the wind, despite the presence of the elders.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra describes Arjuna's skill and predicts the Kuru defeat.
chapters.es: Dhritarashtra admits to Sañjaya that no warrior can withstand the arrows from the gāṇḍīva bow. While Droṇa is an elderly teacher and Karṇa is prone to negligence, Arjuna remains tireless and undefeated. Assisted by his charioteer Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna appears like the god of death. Dhritarashtra envisions the Pāṇḍava warrior’s chariot sound scattering the Kuru forces and his arrows consuming the army like fire in dry grass.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra counts the Pandava strengths and warns of destruction.
chapters.es: Dhritarashtra counts the kings allied with the sons of Pāṇḍu, including the Pañcālas and Matsyas. He identifies Kṛṣṇa as their greatest protector and fears the archery of Sātyaki and Dhṛṣṭadyumna. He admits dread of Yudhiṣṭhira’s restrained anger and Arjuna’s skill. He likens his sons to moths drawn to a fire, warning that a clash will destroy the entire Kuru lineage. Desiring peace, he acknowledges the physical and moral strength of his opponents while doubting his own sons' survival in battle.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya warns Dhritarashtra of the Kurus' coming defeat.
chapters.es: Sanjaya reproaches Dhritarashtra for following his sons despite knowing Arjuna’s power. He reminds the king of his laughter during the gambling match when the Pandavas were exiled. Sanjaya describes Arjuna on a chariot with white horses, holding the gāṇḍīva bow under a monkey banner. Beside him, Krishna wields the sudarśana chakra. He predicts that Bhima and Arjuna will crush the Kuru forces like the wheel of time, noting that many regional kings have already joined the Pandava cause.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana lists his military strengths and predicts victory.
chapters.es: Duryodhana assures Dhṛtarāṣṭra of military victory despite the Pāṇḍavas' alliance with Kṛṣṇa. He contrasts his eleven akṣauhiṇī with the seven divisions of his rivals. Boasting of his training under Saṃkarṣaṇa, he vows to crush Bhīma with a single gadā blow. He lists his commanders, citing Bhīṣma’s power over death, the divine origins of Droṇa and Aśvatthāman, and the śakti weapon held by Karṇa. Citing the counsel of Bṛhaspati regarding superior numbers, he rejects any fear of the coming conflict.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya describes the Pandavas' divine horses and banners.
chapters.es: Sanjaya reports the readiness of the Pandavas and their seven akṣauhiṇī divisions. He describes Arjuna’s chariot and the celestial dhvaja crafted by Tvaṣṭṛ and Bhauvana. This banner shifts colors like a rainbow and moves unimpeded through terrain. Arjuna drives white horses gifted by Citraratha that replace themselves if slain. Bhima, Nakula, and Sahadeva lead teams of ivory, tawny, and speckled horses, while the younger princes ride divine steeds of equal speed and strength.

chapters.subtitle: Sañjaya lists the Pāṇḍava allies and their battlefield targets.
chapters.es: Sañjaya names the allies and divisions gathered for the Pāṇḍavas, including the Vṛṣṇi and Pañcāla forces. The commanders assign specific opponents: Śikhaṇḍī faces Bhīṣma, Bhīma targets Duryodhana, and Arjuna prepares for Karṇa. Dhṛtarāṣṭra describes the kings entering the fire of the gāṇḍīva bow like moths into a flame. Dhṛṣṭadyumna vows to swallow the enemy host like a large fish. He sends a final message via Sañjaya, warning the Kuru elders to seek peace before Arjuna’s divine chariot appears on the field.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana refuses to share land and prepares for war.
chapters.es: Dhṛtarāṣṭra urges his son to cede half the earth, noting that Bhīṣma and Droṇa oppose the conflict. Duryodhana rejects this plea, framing the battle as a raṇayajña where the chariot is the altar and Yudhiṣṭhira is the sacrificial animal. He vows not to yield even as much land as a needle’s tip. Dhṛtarāṣṭra laments the coming carnage, envisioning Bhīmasena laying waste to the Kuru forces like fire consuming a forest, while predicting his son will eventually regret this stubbornness.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya reports Kṛṣṇa’s warning to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
chapters.es: Sanjaya enters the inner chambers and finds Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna reclining on a golden throne, anointed with sandalwood and honey-wine. Arjuna rests Kṛṣṇa’s feet in his lap while his own feet rest on Draupadī and Satyabhāmā. Kṛṣṇa rises to deliver a message for Dhṛtarāṣṭra, advising the Kauravas to perform sacrifices and give charity before war begins. He recalls his debt to Draupadī and asserts that no warrior can overcome Arjuna and his gāṇḍīva bow, citing the battle at Virāṭa as proof.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra urges peace after assessing Arjuna's military power.
chapters.es: Dhṛtarāṣṭra evaluates the military strength of both sides and warns Duryodhana of the pāṇḍava advantage. He recalls Agni’s debt to Arjuna from the khāṇḍava fire and anticipates divine intervention. He describes Arjuna’s gāṇḍīva bow, the inexhaustible quivers, and the monkey-bannered chariot that thunders like clouds. He notes that Arjuna releases five hundred arrows in a single moment, a feat acknowledged by Bhīṣma and Droṇa. Fearing total destruction, the king suffers from insomnia and urges for śama instead of war.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana boasts of his strength and dismisses divine help.
chapters.es: Duryodhana dismisses his father’s fear of divine intervention. He argues that gods remain indifferent to human struggles, noting that the Pāṇḍavas suffered thirteen years without celestial aid. He claims personal control over nature, asserting he can steady the earth with mantra recitations, command jātavedas, and march troops across frozen water. Confident in his mastery of weapons learned from Droṇa and Bhīṣma, he declares that no deity can protect his enemies from destruction once they meet him on the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: Karṇa leaves the court after an argument with Bhīṣma.
chapters.es: Karṇa assures Duryodhana of victory, dismissing the curse Paraśurāma gave him for his deception. He claims he will destroy the Pāṇḍava armies alone. Bhīṣma mocks this boast, reminding the court of Arjuna’s deeds at the Khāṇḍava forest and Kṛṣṇa’s protection. He predicts Karṇa’s śakti weapon will fail against them. Offended by these insults, Karṇa vows to lay down his weapons and avoid the battlefield while Bhīṣma still lives. He leaves the assembly as Bhīṣma continues his critique.

chapters.subtitle: Parables warn against family conflict and reckless ambition.
chapters.es: Duryodhana claims equality with the Pāṇḍava brothers and trusts his own strength to defeat them. A parable describes two birds caught in a net who escape together but fall once they quarrel. Like jñāti who burn together like logs but smoke when separated, family unity ensures survival. Another warning describes mountain honey guarded by serpents on a cliff; Duryodhana pursues the prize of the kingdom but fails to see the sheer drop and the destruction awaiting him.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra warns his son to return the Pandavas' land.
chapters.es: Dhṛtarāṣṭra warns Duryodhana against confronting the Pāṇḍavas and compares their power to the five great elements. Yudhiṣṭhira remains rooted in dharma while Bhīmasena possesses strength comparable to a gale. Arjuna, wielding the gāṇḍīva bow, stands like Mount Meru among peaks. Supported by Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Sātyaki, the brothers find further strength in Kṛṣṇa. Recalling how Arjuna alone scattered the Kuru army at Virāṭa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra urges his son to heed the counsel of Bhīṣma and Droṇa by returning the Pāṇḍavas' share of the kingdom.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna demands the kingdom and threatens the Kuru army.
chapters.es: Arjuna sends formal greetings to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the assembled kings before issuing a final warning to Duryodhana. With eyes red at the corners, he describes the Kuru army as fuel for the impending fire of the Pāṇḍavas. Using the imagery of a sacrifice, he identifies his bow as the ritual ladle and his arrows as the flames. Arjuna demands the return of Yudhiṣṭhira’s share of the kingdom, threatening to drive the enemy host toward death with his chariot and arrows.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya about the strength of both armies.
chapters.es: After the assembly departs, Dhṛtarāṣṭra questions Sañjaya in private about the relative strengths of the rival forces. Seeking an advantage for his sons, the king asks who will survive the coming war. Sañjaya refuses to speak in isolation, fearing the king’s resentment. He requests that Gāndhārī and the elder Vyāsa be present to hear his report. Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana appears and commands Sañjaya to disclose the full truth regarding Vāsudeva and Arjuna to the inquiring king.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna’s cosmic power and his alliance with the Pandavas.
chapters.es: Vasudeva Kṛṣṇa governs the earth and heavens, having defeated Naraka and Kaṃsa as if in play. He outweighs the entire world in strength and turns the kālacakra and yugacakra through his internal power. Wherever truth and dharma exist, Kṛṣṇa remains, ensuring victory. Though he performs deeds like an ordinary laborer, he uses the Pandavas as a sacrificial fire to destroy those who follow adharma. By his māyāyoga, he veils his identity from those who do not seek him.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya explains how to know Krishna through self-control.
chapters.es: Dhritarashtra asks how Sanjaya recognizes the divinity of keśava. Sanjaya explains that vidyā removes the darkness of ignorance, allowing those with pure hearts to see the unborn creator. Duryodhana refuses to seek refuge in Krishna, prompting rebukes from his parents for his pride. Sanjaya instructs the king on indriya-nigraha, the restraint of the senses. He identifies the path to peace as the abandonment of desire and the practice of ahiṃsā, which leads the disciplined mind toward the eternal lord.

chapters.subtitle: Sanjaya explains the meanings of Krishna's many names.
chapters.es: Sañjaya defines the meanings of Kṛṣṇa’s titles for Dhṛtarāṣṭra. He describes Vāsudeva as the dweller within all beings and Mādhava through the practice of silence and meditation. The name Kṛṣṇa unites the roots for earth and joy. As Hṛṣīkeśa, he governs the senses, and as Viṣṇu, he strides across the worlds. Sañjaya concludes that this eternal being, also known as Acyuta, will soon arrive to offer protection and uphold truth.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra praises Krishna before his arrival as a messenger.
chapters.es: Dhritarashtra envies those who will soon see Vāsudeva. He describes the envoy as a light illuminating every direction and a leader of the Yādavas who strips enemies of their fame. He identifies Krishna as the ancient puruṣa and the source of the three worlds, possessing a thousand heads and no beginning or end. Expecting that Krishna’s speech will baffle his own sons while guiding the righteous, Dhritarashtra seeks refuge in this younger brother of Indra.

chapters.subtitle: Yudhiṣṭhira asks Kṛṣṇa to negotiate peace with the Kurus.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira asks Kṛṣṇa to mediate with the Kurus. He offers to settle for five villages like Vāraṇāvata to avoid a war between kinsmen. He explains how greed destroys hrī and leads to the violence of kṣatriya dharma. Comparing combatants to dogs fighting over meat, he emphasizes the futility of victory. Kṛṣṇa agrees to travel to the assembly at Hastināpura, aiming to secure peace and dharma while ensuring the Pāṇḍavas remain protected from the greed of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons.

chapters.subtitle: Kṛṣṇa tells Yudhiṣṭhira to prepare for war.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa urges Yudhiṣṭhira to reject the life of a beggar for the duty of a kṣatriya. He explains that Duryodhana refuses peace, trusting in the power of Bhīṣma and Droṇa. Kṛṣṇa recalls how the Kurus insulted the Pāṇḍavas during the gambling match and their exile. He offers to visit the Kuru court to reveal Duryodhana's greed to all assembled kings. Noting omens of mass death, Kṛṣṇa tells the brothers to ready their weapons, chariots, and elephants for battle.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīma asks Kṛṣṇa to avoid war through negotiation.
chapters.es: Bhīma urges Kṛṣṇa to pursue peace through gentle words rather than threats of war. He describes Duryodhana as a stubborn leader who refuses to bend, likening his anger to a fire that consumes forests. Citing historical examples, he lists eighteen kulapāṃsanāḥ who destroyed their own kin during previous eras. To avoid the total destruction of the Bharatas, Bhīma expresses a willingness to live in a subordinate role, asserting that Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna also prefer reconciliation to battle.

chapters.subtitle: Kṛṣṇa challenges Bhīma’s sudden desire for peace.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa responds to Bhīma’s sudden call for peace with laughter, comparing this mildness to a mountain losing its weight. He recounts Bhīma’s history of restless anger, during which he sighed like smoking fire and uprooted trees. Kṛṣṇa reminds the warrior of his public oath to slay Duryodhana with a gadā. Rejecting this change of heart as a sign of fear, he urges Bhīma to abandon despair and regain his strength for the approaching battle.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīma asserts his strength and readiness for battle.
chapters.es: Bhīmasena rejects Kṛṣṇa’s assessment of his temperament and asserts his physical power. He compares his arms to iron bars, claiming he could hold the earth and sky apart if they collided. While acknowledging that self-praise is unseemly, he vows to crush his enemies underfoot. He explains that his previous restraint was born of a desire to protect his kinsmen rather than fear. In the coming conflict, he promises to strike down elephants and warriors, proving his pauruṣa on the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna discusses destiny and his upcoming peace mission.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa clarifies that his earlier speech intended to rouse Bhīma’s spirit rather than insult his strength. He explains how human effort, or pauruṣa, must contend with the unpredictable forces of daiva. While he prepares to visit the Kuru court to seek a peaceful resolution, he warns that victory in battle remains uncertain. Kṛṣṇa commits to serving as the charioteer for Arjuna if negotiations fail. He places the burden of the coming conflict upon the shoulders of Bhīma and Arjuna.

chapters.subtitle: Bhima tells Krishna to choose the best path.
chapters.es: Bhīmasena clarifies his position following Kṛṣṇa’s critique. He admits that Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s greed and the memory of Draupadī’s public humiliation make a peaceful settlement unlikely. Comparing Duryodhana to barren soil where no seed of counsel can grow, he acknowledges that the enemy deserves death. He grants Kṛṣṇa the authority to use either gentle means or force to protect the Pāṇḍavas’ interests. He urges a swift resolution to the conflict to safeguard their remaining honor.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna explains the balance between effort and fate.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa compares the union of human effort and destiny to a farmer preparing a field that requires rain to yield fruit. He pledges to apply his full puruṣakāra while acknowledging that daiva is unpredictable. He describes Duryodhana as a ruler who, led by Śakuni and Karṇa, refuses to return the kingdom. Kṛṣṇa resolves to seek a peaceful settlement in the Kuru assembly to honor Yudhiṣṭhira’s wishes, though he expects Duryodhana’s stubbornness will make conflict unavoidable.

chapters.subtitle: Sahadeva advises Krishna on the mission to the Kauravas.
chapters.es: Sahadeva tells Kṛṣṇa that human intent shifts with circumstance. While the Pāṇḍavas sought little in the forest, they now stand with seven akṣauhiṇī armies. He names warriors like Sātyaki, Virāṭa, and Drupada who wait with raised weapons. Sahadeva asks Kṛṣṇa to use words that seem peaceful but stir fear in Duryodhana. He expects Vidura, Bhīṣma, and Droṇa to support this message before King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, ensuring Kṛṣṇa acts according to the needs of the present time.

chapters.subtitle: Satyaki demands war to avenge the Pandavas
chapters.es: Sātyaki rejects Yudhiṣṭhira’s call for peace and urges Kṛṣṇa to incite war against the Kurus. He insists that his manyu, or fury, remains unappeased after the public humiliation of Draupadī in the assembly hall. Recalling the sight of the Pāṇḍavas dressed in deerskins during their exile, he supports Sahadeva’s demand for Duryodhana’s death. The gathered warriors roar in approval, confirming that the army prefers battle over negotiation. They cheer the son of Śini, signaling their collective intent to engage on the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: Draupadī shows Kṛṣṇa her hair and demands war.
chapters.es: Draupadī addresses Kṛṣṇa before he departs to negotiate a settlement, recounting her public humiliation. She describes being dragged into the assembly by her hair while the Pāṇḍavas watched. Seizing her dark locks with her left hand, she demands that Kṛṣṇa remember this insult during his mission. She rejects peace and insists on the death of Duḥśāsana and his brothers. Kṛṣṇa consoles the weeping queen, vowing that his words are certain and that she will soon see her enemies slain on the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: Kṛṣṇa departs for Hastinapura to negotiate for peace.
chapters.es: Under the Revatī asterism, Kṛṣṇa completes his morning rituals, circumambulates the sacred fire, and touches a bull. He mounts his gold-decked chariot, carrying his cakra and gadā while the Garuḍa banner flies above. Escorted briefly by the Pāṇḍavas, he receives Yudhiṣṭhira’s messages for Kuntī and the Kuru elders. Arjuna reaffirms their demand for half the kingdom as Bhīma roars. On the road, Kṛṣṇa greets a gathering of sages who follow him to hear his speech in the royal assembly.

chapters.subtitle: Kṛṣṇa travels toward Hastināpura and rests at Vṛkasthala.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa departs for Hastināpura accompanied by ten charioteers and infantry. While violent storms and earthquakes strike the Kuru capital, his specific path remains peaceful with blooming flowers and smooth ground. He travels through prosperous lands where villagers gather to see him. Reaching Vṛkasthala at sunset, he performs his evening sandhyā prayers. After his charioteer Dāruka tends the horses, Kṛṣṇa accepts the hospitality and food offered by local Brāhmaṇas, choosing to rest there for the night before continuing his mission.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra orders preparations for Krishna's arrival.
chapters.es: King Dhṛtarāṣṭra prepares for the arrival of Kṛṣṇa by ordering the construction of pavilions along the road. Duryodhana stocks these rest-houses with gems, fine garments, and fragrant garlands, establishing a primary residence at Vṛkasthala. The king instructs his sons to treat the envoy with honors due to a sovereign. However, Kṛṣṇa travels past these sites without stopping to inspect the offerings, continuing his journey directly toward the Kuru capital to represent the Pāṇḍavas.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra prepares gifts and a reception for Krishna's arrival.
chapters.es: Dhṛtarāṣṭra announces the arrival of Janārdana from Vṛkasthala and prepares a reception. He lists offerings of sixteen gold chariots drawn by black horses, eight trained elephants, and thousands of mountain-bred blankets and deer skins. He orders the city streets cleared of dust and decorated with banners. Duśśāsana’s residence is refurbished to house the guest. The king commands his sons and the city’s women to meet the envoy on the road, while the citizens gather to witness his entry into the capital.

chapters.subtitle: Vidura warns the King against trying to bribe Krishna.
chapters.es: Vidura rejects Dhritarashtra’s plan to offer Krishna extravagant wealth. He views these gifts as a deceptive attempt to bribe the envoy and isolate him from the Pandavas. Vidura insists that Janārdana is inseparable from Dhanañjaya and values simple hospitality, like water for the feet, over riches. He advises the King to abandon these schemes and instead grant the five villages requested by the brothers. By acting as a father to both sides, the King should choose śama to settle the dispute.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana plans to capture Kṛṣṇa during his peace mission.
chapters.es: Duryodhana rejects the proposal to offer gifts to Kṛṣṇa, fearing the gesture signals cowardice. He argues that peace is unattainable without conflict and plots to imprison Kṛṣṇa upon his arrival. By binding the envoy, he intends to force the Pāṇḍavas and their allies into submission. Dhṛtarāṣṭra warns against harming a messenger, while Bhīṣma denounces the scheme as ruinous. Offended by the suggestion of such a crime, Bhīṣma abandons the assembly, leaving the king to contemplate his son's malice.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna arrives in Hastinapura and visits King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
chapters.es: Krishna departs Vṛkasthala after his morning rites and travels to Hastināpura. Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the Kuru princes meet him on the road, while Duryodhana remains behind. Crowds fill the decorated streets and lean from balconies, making the horses halt. In the white palace, Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the elders rise from their seats to offer Krishna madhuparka and a golden chair. After formal greetings, Krishna leaves the court for Vidura’s residence, where he shares news of the Pāṇḍavas.

chapters.subtitle: Kunti tells Krishna her sons must fulfill their duty.
chapters.es: Janārdana visits Pṛthā, who weeps while recalling her sons' exile. She contrasts their former life of luxury—waking to drums and Vedic chants—with the harsh sounds of the forest. Recounting the humiliation of Kṛṣṇā in the assembly, she urges her sons to fulfill the Kṣatriya duty for which she bore them. She tells Govinda that the time for action has arrived. Kṛṣṇa comforts her, promising that her sons will soon rule again, before departing for the palace of Duryodhana.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna rejects Duryodhana's food to dine with Vidura.
chapters.es: After visiting Pṛthā, Kṛṣṇa enters Duryodhana's palace and sits upon a golden couch. He rejects the king's invitation to dine, explaining that messengers eat only after their mission is complete. He states that one accepts food through friendship or in distress; since Duryodhana hates the virtuous Pāṇḍavas, his food is defiled. Declaring his unity with the sons of Pāṇḍu, Kṛṣṇa leaves the assembly. He goes to Vidura's house, where he honors Brāhmaṇas and eats pure anna with his followers.

chapters.subtitle: Vidura warns Krishna about Duryodhana's refusal to make peace
chapters.es: After dining, Vidura warns Kṛṣṇa against visiting the Kuru court. He describes Duryodhana as a man driven by kāma and krodha who ignores the counsel of elders. Confident in Karṇa and a massive army, Duryodhana rejects peace. Vidura compares offering wise words to these men to singing for the deaf. He notes that the assembled kings harbor ancient grudges against Kṛṣṇa and fears for his safety among vengeful men who hate the Pāṇḍava brothers.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna explains his reasons for attempting a peace mission.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa explains his arrival to Vidura, acknowledging the hostility of the Kurus. He seeks to release the earth from the mṛtyupāśa, or noose of death, through a sincere attempt at peace. He maintains that a person who strives for dharma gains merit even if the effort fails. By intervening, he avoids future blame for failing to prevent the slaughter. He intends to speak words of artha to Duryodhana while protecting the rights of the Pāṇḍavas. Finally, he rests.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna enters the Kuru assembly hall.
chapters.es: Krishna wakes to the sound of conchs and drums. After performing morning rituals and distributing gifts to brāhmaṇas, he mounts his gem-studded chariot. Duryodhana and Śakuni escort him through streets lined with spectators on balconies. In the assembly hall, Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Bhīṣma rise to honor him. Before sitting on his golden throne, Krishna ensures that Nārada and other sages are seated with due respect. The assembly falls silent as everyone gazes at his form adorned with the kaustubha gem and yellow silk.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna asks the Kuru king to make peace.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa stands before the silent assembly and addresses Dhṛtarāṣṭra with a voice like a deep drum. He seeks śama to prevent the slaughter of the warrior class and the ruin of the earth. He urges the monarch to restrain his greedy sons and restore the ancestral share of the kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas. Highlighting the completed thirteen years of exile, Kṛṣṇa warns the court that justice must prevail, as the brothers are equally prepared to serve their elders or strike on the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: A proud king is defeated by an ascetic’s grass.
chapters.es: King Dambhodbhava, a monarch blinded by pride, seeks a match in combat and travels to Mount Gandhamādana to challenge the ascetics Nara and Nārāyaṇa. Faced with a full army and clouds of arrows, Nara counters with only a handful of iṣīkā grass. These blades blind and deafen the king's soldiers, compelling him to yield. Jamadagnya explains that this ancient pair now walks the earth as Arjuna and Janārdana, wielding weapons that no mortal army can withstand.

chapters.subtitle: Kaṇva advises Duryodhana and describes Matali’s journey to Nagaloka.
chapters.es: Kaṇva advises Duryodhana to seek peace with the Pandavas, who possess divine power. He notes that while Viṣṇu and the twin sages Nara-Nārāyaṇa remain eternal, kings and physical elements eventually perish. To illustrate his counsel, Kaṇva recounts the search of Matali, Indra's charioteer, for a husband for his daughter, Guṇakeśī. Rejecting suitors among gods and men, Matali leaves his wife, Sudharmā, to search the subterranean realm of the nāga spirits for a worthy match.

chapters.subtitle: Narada and Matali visit Varuna's kingdom for a groom.
chapters.es: Matali meets Narada while seeking a husband for his daughter. Together, they enter the underwater kingdom of Varuna. Narada points out the god’s sons and the residence of Jyotsnākālī. They observe weapons seized from the Daityas, the vaiṣṇava discus, and the gāṇḍīva bow. Narada shows Matali the first staff of punishment created by Brahma and Varuna’s umbrella, which sheds cool water like a raincloud. After viewing these sights, they proceed deeper into the world of the serpents.

chapters.subtitle: Narada describes the subterranean realm of Patala to Matali.
chapters.es: Pātāla sits at the center of the serpent world, housing defeated Daityas and a submarine fire that consumes water. Here, gods stored amṛta, and the elephant Airāvata draws moisture to supply Indra’s rain clouds. Moonlight revives inhabitants at night, while sages practicing the govrata vow dwell alongside diverse aquatic life. An unidentified glowing egg remains submerged, destined to release a fire that destroys the universe at time’s end. Mātali observes these sights but finds no suitable husband for his daughter.

chapters.subtitle: Matali rejects a groom from the city of Hiranyapura.
chapters.es: Narada leads Matali to the subterranean city of Hiranyapura, a stronghold built for the Daityas and Danavas. Palaces crafted from gold, silver, and vaiḍūrya rise like mountains, housing the Nivātakavacas and other warriors who remain undefeated by the gods. Narada invites Matali to select a husband for his daughter from among these inhabitants. Matali refuses, citing the perpetual enmity between the gods and the Danavas. He rejects an alliance with the enemy and asks to continue their search in another realm.

chapters.subtitle: Narada describes the bird race to Matali.
chapters.es: Nārada describes the region of the suparṇa birds to Mātali. These descendants of Kaśyapa and Vinatā sustain themselves by consuming snakes and bear the śrīvatsa mark. Though they act with the ferocity of kṣatriya warriors, they remain devoted to Viṣṇu. The lineage includes figures such as Sumukha and Vāmana, known for tireless flight and strength. Mātali observes their traits and names before deciding whether a suitable husband for his daughter resides within this divine race.

chapters.subtitle: Matali describes the seventh earth and the cow Surabhi.
chapters.es: Rasātala constitutes the seventh layer of the earth where the cow Surabhi dwells. Born from the mouth of Pitāmaha, her milk forms the Kṣīranidhi ocean. Sages called Phenapa subsist on the foam of this milk while practicing austerities. Four cows—Surūpā, Haṃsakā, Subhadrā, and Sarvakāmadughā—support the cardinal directions. From their milk, the churning of the ocean produced amṛta, Lakṣmī, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, and the Kaustubha gem. Inhabitants claim this realm provides more happiness than the world of the gods.

chapters.subtitle: Matali chooses a serpent prince for his daughter.
chapters.es: Nārada leads Mātali through the city of Bhogavatī, where the serpent Śeṣa supports the earth. Many serpents dwell here, bearing marks of jewels and svastika signs on their hoods. Mātali observes Sumukha, a descendant of Airāvata and grandson of Āryaka. Though the eagle Garuḍa recently killed Sumukha’s father Chikura, the youth’s poise impresses the visitor. Recognizing his lineage and appearance, Mātali selects Sumukha as the husband for his daughter Guṇakeśī and resolves to arrange the marriage.

chapters.subtitle: Indra grants the Naga Sumukha long life and marriage.
chapters.es: Nārada proposes a marriage between Mātali’s daughter, Guṇakeśī, and the nāga Sumukha. Sumukha’s grandfather, Āryaka, hesitates because Garuḍa has vowed to devour the youth within a month. To protect the groom, Mātali and Nārada lead Sumukha to the court of Indra where Viṣṇu is present. Viṣṇu suggests granting the nāga immortality, but Indra instead bestows a long lifespan. Secured from Garuḍa’s threat, Sumukha weds Guṇakeśī and returns to his home. The sages and gods depart, having finalized the union.

chapters.subtitle: Vishnu humbles Garuda and Duryodhana ignores the warning.
chapters.es: Angered when Indra spares a serpent, Garuḍa boasts he can carry the world on one wing. Viṣṇu tests this pride by resting his right arm on the bird’s shoulder. The weight crushes Garuḍa to the ground, forcing him to shed his feathers and realize his limits. Viṣṇu pardons the humbled bird, but when Kaṇva retells this to Duryodhana as a warning, the prince slaps his thigh and rejects the lesson, remaining committed to war against the Pāṇḍavas.

chapters.subtitle: Viśvāmitra demands eight hundred rare horses from Galava.
chapters.es: Dharma tests Viśvāmitra’s discipline by visiting his hermitage disguised as the sage Vasiṣṭha. Viśvāmitra stands motionless for a century, carrying a vessel of hot rice on his head while the student Galava tends to him. After Dharma grants Viśvāmitra brāhmaṇatva, the sage permits Galava to depart. However, Galava repeatedly insists on offering gurudakṣiṇā. Provoked by this stubbornness, Viśvāmitra demands a fee of eight hundred moon-white horses, each distinguished by a single black ear.

chapters.subtitle: Gālava despairs and Garuḍa offers to help him.
chapters.es: Gālava wastes away to skin and bones, refusing food and sleep after Viśvāmitra demands eight hundred moon-white horses as gurudakṣiṇā. Burdened by debt and the weight of a broken promise, he contemplates ending his life or seeking refuge with Viṣṇu. His friend Garuḍa arrives to intervene, offering his wings to transport Gālava across the earth. The bird-deity pledges his strength to help his companion find the rare steeds and satisfy the sage's difficult command.

chapters.subtitle: Matali describes the importance of the eastern direction.
chapters.es: Mātali offers to convey Gālava toward any cardinal point, beginning with a description of the east. This region marks the sunrise and the penance of the sādhya deities. Here, the daughters of Dakṣa produced offspring, and Indra received his royal consecration. The Vedas were first chanted in this quarter, and the sun bestowed the yajus verses upon teachers. As the gateway to the three worlds, the east houses the origins of the oṃkāra and the ancestral seat of the sage Vasiṣṭha.

chapters.subtitle: Garuḍa describes the southern direction to the sage Gālava.
chapters.es: Vivasvat offered the southern quarter as a gift to his preceptor. The pitṛs and viśvedevas dwell here, where time is measured in truṭi and lava. The River Vaitaraṇī flows through this region, and the sun releases its cool moisture. Within the city of Bhogavatī, the serpents Vāsuki and Takṣaka reside. Rāvaṇa performed penance here, and the sage Kapila destroyed the sons of Sagara. Gandharvas sing in the Mandara groves while souls journey toward this gate of dharma.

chapters.subtitle: The geography and legends of the western direction
chapters.es: Varuṇa rules the western quarter where the sun sets behind Mount Asta. From here, night and sleep emerge to claim half of human life. Soma drinks the juices of the ocean to regain youth each month. The region houses the dwellings of Viṣṇu, Kaśyapa, and the serpent Ananta. Indra divided Diti’s womb here, creating the maruts. Surabhi sheds milk near golden mountains, the headless trunk of Rāhu remains visible in the sea, and the sun’s path turns sideways.

chapters.subtitle: Mātali describes the landmarks and residents of the north.
chapters.es: The northern direction, known as uttarā, serves as the site where Nārāyaṇa and Nara dwell at the badarī hermitage. On the slopes of the himavat, Maheśvara receives the falling Gaṅgā and Kubera rules the yakṣa tribes from Kailāsa. The Saptarṣi and Arundhatī remain fixed in this quarter, while the sun and moon revolve around the central axis. Here, Viṣṇu left his footprint during his three strides, and the lokapāla guardians announce their protection every morning and evening.

chapters.subtitle: Garuda carries Galava east to find specific horses.
chapters.es: Galava mounts Garuda to travel toward the east. The wind from the bird’s wings churns the ocean, lifting timingila fish and nāga from the depths. Blinded by the speed and the roar of the sea, Galava loses sight of the sun and the sky. He confesses his despair over finding eight hundred white horses with black ears for his teacher's fee. Garuda laughs at his fear and lands on Mount Ṛṣabha to rest before continuing their search.

chapters.subtitle: Garuda loses his feathers after insulting an ascetic.
