chapters.es: Garuḍa and Gālava land on Ṛṣabha mountain to rest with the ascetic Śāṇḍilī. After eating her food, Garuḍa plans to carry the woman to the celestial realms of Viṣṇu and Mahādeva. This mental slight causes his feathers to fall off, leaving him a bare mass of flesh. Śāṇḍilī explains that her power derives from ācāra, or proper conduct, and warns him against judging women. She restores his wings before the pair encounters Viśvāmitra, who demands the payment of Gālava’s debt.

chapters.subtitle: Garuda asks King Yayāti to help Gālava find horses.
chapters.es: Garuda consoles the despondent Gālava by explaining the divine origins of wealth and the difficulty of acquiring it. He leads the brahmin to the city of Pratiṣṭhāna to seek help from King Yayāti. Garuda introduces Gālava as a student of Viśvāmitra who must provide eight hundred moon-white horses with one black ear, known as śyāmakarṇa, as his gurudakṣiṇā. He asks the king to grant this request, comparing the union of a worthy giver and receiver to milk held in a conch shell.

chapters.subtitle: Yayāti gives his daughter to Gālava for horses.
chapters.es: Yayāti receives Gālava and Garuḍa but admits his treasury is depleted. To prevent the sage from leaving empty-handed, he offers his daughter, Mādhavī, whose appearance ensures a high śulka, or bride-price. He suggests that kings will trade the required śyāmakarṇa horses for her hand. Gālava accepts the princess and travels to Ayodhyā. There, he presents Mādhavī to King Haryaśva, proposing a marriage in exchange for the rare steeds needed to fulfill his obligation to his preceptor.

chapters.subtitle: A king trades horses for a son with Mādhavī.
chapters.es: King Haryaśva identifies physical marks on Mādhavī that signify she will bear a great ruler. Gālava requests eight hundred white horses with black ears, but the king holds only two hundred. Mādhavī shares that a boon allows her to return to a maiden state after childbirth. Gālava accepts the two hundred horses, and Haryaśva fathers a son named Vasumanas. Fulfilling the agreement, Gālava later takes the girl from the palace to seek the next king, Divodāsa, for the remaining debt.

chapters.subtitle: Gālava gives Mādhavī to Divodāsa for two hundred horses
chapters.es: Gālava leads Mādhavī to Divodāsa, the king of Kāśī, offering her for two hundred horses. The king accepts the terms and performs the marriage rites. After their union, Mādhavī gives birth to a son named Pratardana. Once the child is born, Gālava returns to the palace to collect the princess. Abiding by the original agreement, the king restores Mādhavī to the sage so he may seek the remaining horses from another ruler.

chapters.subtitle: Gālava trades Mādhvī to King Uśīnara for special horses.
chapters.es: Gālava leads Mādhvī to King Uśīnara in Bhojanagara to obtain white horses with black ears. He offers her as a wife to pay his teacher’s debt. Uśīnara owns only two hundred such steeds and agrees to father one son, refusing to spend his kingdom’s wealth on himself. After living in mountain caves and palaces, Mādhvī bears a son named Śibi. Gālava takes her back and meets Garuḍa to discuss their progress.

chapters.subtitle: Galava pays his debt using Madhavi and the horses.
chapters.es: Garuḍa explains that the remaining śyāmakarṇa horses were lost in the Vitastā river. He advises Gālava to offer the six hundred horses already gathered along with Mādhavī to Viśvāmitra. Viśvāmitra accepts the maiden in place of the final two hundred horses. He begets a son, Aṣṭaka, and returns Mādhavī to Gālava. Having fulfilled the debt of his guru-dakṣiṇā, Gālava restores the maiden to her father, Yayāti, and retires to the forest to practice austerities.

chapters.subtitle: Madhavi chooses a forest life and Yayati loses merit.
chapters.es: King Yayāti organizes a svayaṃvara for Mādhavī at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. Rejecting all suitors, Mādhavī enters the forest to live as a hermit. She adopts the habits of a deer, grazing on grass and drinking from forest streams. Meanwhile, Yayāti ascends to heaven, but his pride leads him to insult the gods and sages. His celestial luster fades as his merit fails, and the inhabitants of heaven begin to question his identity and right to remain there.

chapters.subtitle: King Yayāti falls from heaven and meets his grandsons.
chapters.es: King Yayāti falls from heaven after his merit is exhausted by pride. His withered garlands and slipping crown mark his descent. He plunges through sacrificial smoke toward the Naimiṣa forest, landing among four kings performing the vājapeya rite. Though they offer him their religious merit, Yayāti refuses charity as a kṣatriya. His daughter Mādhavī arrives, identifying the kings as his grandsons. These kings and the sage Gālava then offer their gathered tapas to help him ascend back to the celestial realm.

chapters.subtitle: Four grandsons give their merit to save Yayati.
chapters.es: Yayati regains his celestial form, wearing divine garlands and jewels. His feet no longer touch the earth. His grandsons—Vasumanas, Pratardana, Shibi, and Ashtaka—offer him the merit of their virtuous deeds. Vasumanas provides the fruits of his charity, Pratardana gives his rewards for valor, Shibi offers the power of his truthfulness, and Ashtaka contributes his sacrificial rewards. As they speak, Yayati rises from the ground. Supported by the dharma of his daughter's sons, the king ascends back to the heavens.

chapters.subtitle: King Yayāti returns to heaven and learns about pride.
chapters.es: Yayāti ascends to the celestial realm supported by the merit of his grandsons. Rain of flowers and the music of dundubhi drums greet him as he regains his eternal station. Brahmā explains that his earlier fall resulted from abhimāna, or pride, which clouded his mind. He instructs the king that heaven remains closed to those using deceit or violence. He states that every person eventually reaps the fruits of their own sacrifices, gifts, and penance.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna advises Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas.
chapters.es: Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks Kṛṣṇa to reason with his son. Kṛṣṇa urges Duryodhana to choose peace to save the Kuru lineage. He contrasts the dharma of the Pāṇḍavas with Duryodhana’s reliance on wicked advisors. Citing the trivarga, Kṛṣṇa explains that only righteous conduct secures power. He recounts Arjuna’s victories at Khāṇḍavaprastha and Virāṭa to prove the Pāṇḍavas’ strength. Finally, Kṛṣṇa offers Duryodhana the position of crown prince if he grants the Pāṇḍavas their half of the kingdom.

chapters.subtitle: Elders urge Duryodhana to accept Krishna’s peace offer.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma urges Duryodhana to heed the words of Keśava to protect the Bharata lineage. Droṇa warns that the force of Arjuna and Vāsudeva is invincible and cautions him against the advice of foolish men. Vidura laments the fate of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, predicting they will wander like wingless birds in their old age. Finally, Dhṛtarāṣṭra himself implores his son to seek a settlement with Yudhiṣṭhira, viewing the offer of peace as a final chance for safety.

chapters.subtitle: Elders advise Duryodhana to make peace with his cousins.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma and Droṇa urge Duryodhana to seek peace before Arjuna draws the Gāṇḍīva bow and Kṛṣṇa prepares for combat. They describe a pending slaughter where Bhīmasena’s mace strikes down heads like ripe fruit and arrows pierce chests scented with sandalwood. Instead of battle, they envision Yudhiṣṭhira embracing his cousin and Bhīmasena speaking words of reconciliation. They advise Duryodhana to unite with his brothers, allowing the assembled kings to witness a joyful reunion and share the earth in peace.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana refuses to give land to the Pandavas.
chapters.es: Duryodhana defends his conduct before the Kuru assembly, denying any fault in the dyūta where the Pandavas lost their kingdom to Shakuni. He identifies the warrior’s highest duty as falling on the battlefield rather than bowing to enemies. Citing the kṣatradharma of standing tall despite ruin, he refuses to restore the territory Dhritarashtra surrendered in the past. He concludes by vowing not to yield even as much land as a sharp needle’s point (sūcyāgra) to his cousins.

chapters.subtitle: Kṛṣṇa tells the Kuru elders to arrest Duryodhana.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa confronts Duryodhana in the assembly, listing the poisoning of the Pāṇḍavas and the public humiliation of Draupadī after the akṣadyūtam. Duryodhana stalks out in anger, rejecting the counsel of Bhīṣma and his own parents. Kṛṣṇa then urges the Kuru elders to seize Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni. Recalling his execution of Kaṃsa for the Yādava clan, he advocates for sacrificing one individual to preserve the family. He asks the elders to hand over the conspirators to avoid a total kṣatriya slaughter.

chapters.subtitle: Gandhari tells Duryodhana to share the kingdom.
chapters.es: Dhrtarastra summons Gandhari to the assembly to restrain their son. Duryodhana enters with red eyes, hissing like a snake. Gandhari rebukes Dhrtarastra’s indulgence and warns Duryodhana that an undisciplined king is like a driver of uncurbed horses. She compares kāma and krodha to a net that entangles fish, clouding judgment. She urges him to share the kingdom with the Pandavas, insisting that mastery of the self precedes mastery of the earth, as war offers no certain victory or lasting happiness.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana plots to seize Kṛṣṇa and faces rebuke.
chapters.es: Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni plot to seize Kṛṣṇa to demoralize the Pāṇḍava army. Sātyaki discovers the scheme and stations Kṛtavarman’s troops at the assembly gates. Vidura and Dhṛtarāṣṭra rebuke Duryodhana, comparing his plan to a child reaching for the moon or a moth flying into a flame. Vidura recounts Kṛṣṇa’s past deeds, including the slaying of Kaṃsa and the lifting of Govardhana. Kṛṣṇa informs Dhṛtarāṣṭra that he could easily restrain the conspirators but refuses to act out of malice.

chapters.subtitle: Kṛṣṇa reveals his divine form to the Kuru assembly.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa responds to Duryodhana’s attempt to seize him by revealing his universal form. Fire and smoke erupt from his eyes and pores as deities like Brahmā and Rudra appear on his body. The Pāṇḍava brothers and Vṛṣṇi warriors emerge with raised weapons while the earth trembles. While most kings turn away in terror, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Vidura receive divine sight to witness the manifestation. Kṛṣṇa eventually withdraws the form and departs the assembly to visit Pṛthā.

chapters.subtitle: Kunti urges Yudhiṣṭhira to fight for his kingdom.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa visits Kunti to report the failure of peace negotiations in the Kuru assembly. Kunti delivers a stern message for Yudhiṣṭhira, rebuking his preference for monastic quietude over kṣatradharma. She asserts that a king's conduct of daṇḍanīti defines the era, declaring that the ruler causes the time, whether kṛtayuga or kaliyuga. Citing the example of Muchukunda, she commands her sons to reclaim their paternal inheritance through strength and battle rather than subsisting on the charity of their rivals.

chapters.subtitle: A mother encourages her son to fight his enemies.
chapters.es: Vidurā rebukes her son Sañjaya as he lies dejected after his defeat by the King of Sindhu. She rejects his self-pity, comparing him to a corpse or a mouse satisfied by a tiny drink. She commands him to rise and display his vīrya. Using the image of a tinduka ember, she insists that it is better to flare up for a single moment than to smoke forever. She urges him to harden his heart like iron and reclaim his lost kingdom.

chapters.subtitle: A mother urges her son to reclaim his kingdom.
chapters.es: Vidula commands Sañjaya to abandon his despondency and reclaim his royal status. She warns that a kṣatriya who clings to life instead of showing valor lives as a thief. Describing poverty as a living death, she urges him to rise like a blazing ulmuka against the King of Sindhu. She invokes Indra’s victory over Vṛtra as a model for action. Sañjaya must bow only to dharma and the gods, choosing to break like a branch rather than submit to an enemy.

chapters.subtitle: Vidulā teaches Sañjaya how to rebuild his power.
chapters.es: Sañjaya accuses his mother, Vidulā, of possessing a heart forged from kṛṣṇāyasa for demanding he risk his life. He questions the worth of sovereignty bought with a son’s blood. Vidulā rejects his plea as misplaced pity, which she likens to the aimless affection of a donkey. She commands him to exert pauruṣa despite his lack of wealth. By recruiting the disgruntled and honoring allies, he must pursue victory, as a kṣatriya finds no peace except through the defeat of enemies.

chapters.subtitle: A mother urges her son to reclaim his kingdom.
chapters.es: Vidula warns that a king who shows fear loses his kingdom as allies and ministers defect. She reveals a hidden kośa and a circle of loyal friends to support a new campaign. Driven by her arrow-like words, Sanjaya discards his despair and likens her to a driver steering through deep water. He resolves to strike his enemies. This history, known as Jaya, strengthens those seeking victory and promotes the birth of heroic sons.

chapters.subtitle: Kunti sends a message and Krishna departs from Hastinapura.
chapters.es: Kuntī recalls the celestial voice at Arjuna’s birth predicting his conquest of the Kurus. She charges Kṛṣṇa to remind her sons that a kṣatriya woman bears children for the sake of battle. She identifies the public insult of Draupadī in the assembly as her primary sorrow, urging Bhīma and Arjuna to reclaim their share of the kingdom through valor. Kṛṣṇa departs the city, taking Karṇa in his chariot for a private discussion, while the Kuru elders contemplate the coming destruction.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma and Drona urge Duryodhana to make peace.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma and Droṇa urge Duryodhana to accept peace following Kunti’s message. They remind him of Arjuna’s strength at Virāṭa and his rescue of the Kauravas during the ghoṣayātrā. They envision a reconciliation where Yudhiṣṭhira embraces his brother and the kings shed tears of joy. Citing ill omens like circling vultures and falling meteors, they warn that refusal will lead to slaughter. They predict he will regret his pride once he hears the sound of the gāṇḍīva and Bhīma’s roar in battle.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma and Drona urge the king to avoid war.
chapters.es: Bhishma and Drona observe the king’s downcast face and furrowed brow. Drona speaks of the pain of fighting dhanañjaya, a student he loves as much as his own son. He questions a kṣatriya code that compels such a clash. The elders warn that the Pandavas possess the counsel of janārdana and the support of the gods. They point to Draupadi’s ascetic power as a sign of victory and urge the king to choose peace over the destruction of his lineage.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna offers Karna the throne as the oldest brother.
chapters.es: Krishna takes Karṇa into his chariot and reveals his identity as the eldest son of Kuntī. Citing dharmaśāstra rules regarding children born to unmarried women, Krishna identifies him as the legal heir to Pāṇḍu. He offers Karṇa the kingship, describing an abhiṣeka on a tiger skin where Yudhiṣṭhira carries the white fan and Bhīmasena holds the royal umbrella. Krishna promises that the Pāṇḍava brothers and the Vṛṣṇi clans will follow his chariot as he rules the kingdom.

chapters.subtitle: Karna remains loyal to Duryodhana despite his royal birth.
chapters.es: Karṇa acknowledges his birth to Kuntī and Sūrya but remains with the foster parents who raised him. He refuses to abandon Duryodhana, whose support sustains his family. Fearing Yudhiṣṭhira might forfeit the throne upon learning the truth, Karṇa asks Kṛṣṇa to hide his identity. He describes the approaching battle as a yajña, an offering where weapons serve as sacrificial tools and blood as the oblation. He accepts his fate to fall against Arjuna, seeking a warrior’s death on Kurukṣetra.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna warns Karna and sets the date for war
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa warns Karṇa of the certain Pāṇḍava victory, describing the terrifying celestial illusions on Arjuna’s vānara banner. He foretells the end of the earlier ages as Bhīma drinks the blood of Duḥśāsana and the Pāṇḍava brothers overwhelm the Kuru forces. Kṛṣṇa instructs Karṇa to inform Bhīṣma and Droṇa that the battle should commence in seven days on the amāvāsyā night. He concludes by promising that the kings aligned with Duryodhana will find their final passage through death on the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: Karna foretells the Kurus' defeat through omens and dreams.
chapters.es: Karna describes celestial portents signaling the destruction of the Kauravas. He observes the planet Śanaiścara troubling the constellations and notes how vultures follow Duryodhana’s troops while auspicious birds attend the Pandavas. Recounting a dream, Karna sees Yudhishthira ascending a white palace and Arjuna riding a celestial elephant with Krishna. He views himself, Bhīṣma, and Droṇa riding camels toward the south, the region of death. Resigned to the slaughter, Karna embraces Krishna and departs to face his fate.

chapters.subtitle: Kunti meets Karna on the river bank.
chapters.es: Vidura visits Kuntī to lament the approaching war and Duryodhana’s refusal to seek peace. Worried by Karṇa’s enmity toward her sons, Kuntī remembers the mantra received from Durvāsā and her secret summoning of the sun god. She resolves to reveal Karṇa’s identity as her firstborn to prevent the slaughter of kin. Kuntī finds him on the banks of the Bhagirathī, standing with upraised arms facing the east. She waits in the sun's heat until he concludes his prayers and greets her.

chapters.subtitle: Kuntī tells Karṇa the truth about his birth.
chapters.es: Karṇa greets Kuntī as the son of Adhiratha. She reveals he is her first-born son, conceived through the sun god Sūrya in the house of Kuntibhoja. Born wearing kavaca and kuṇḍala, he is a kānīna child and the eldest Pāṇḍava. Kuntī urges him to abandon the Dhārtarāṣṭras to reclaim royal fortune alongside Yudhiṣṭhira. She asks him to join his five brothers, ending the label of sūtaputra and uniting with Arjuna like the pair of Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa.

chapters.subtitle: Karna promises Kunti he will only fight Arjuna.
chapters.es: Sūrya urges Karṇa to obey Kuntī, but Karṇa remains firm. He rebukes Kuntī for abandoning him as an infant, an act that stripped him of his kṣatriya rites. Refusing to desert Duryodhana, Karṇa views himself as the vessel for the Kauravas to cross the coming war. He pledges to spare Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and the twins, limiting his lethal intent to Arjuna. This vow ensures Kuntī retains five sons regardless of who falls in their duel. Grieved by the fate of the Kurus, Kuntī accepts and departs.

chapters.subtitle: Krishna reports Bhishma's speech about the royal succession.
chapters.es: Kṛṣṇa returns to Upaplavya and reports the failed peace mission to the Pāṇḍavas. He recounts how Bhīṣma addressed the assembly, detailing his own renunciation of the throne for his father, Śantanu. Bhīṣma describes refusing the crown despite the pleas of the subjects during a time of famine. He explains that Pāṇḍu rightfully ruled because Dhṛtarāṣṭra was blind. Consequently, Bhīṣma commands Duryodhana to give the Pāṇḍavas their half of the kingdom, asserting that they are the legitimate heirs to the Kuru lineage.

chapters.subtitle: Elders advise Duryodhana to share the kingdom with Pāṇḍavas.
chapters.es: Droṇa reminds the assembly how Pāṇḍu handed the Kuru throne to Dhṛtarāṣṭra before retreating to the woods. He insists that Duryodhana share the kingdom, stating yato dharmastato jayaḥ. Vidura warns of the destruction of the lineage and proposes restraining the prince to preserve the state. Gāndhārī then enters the hall to condemn her son's greed. She identifies Yudhiṣṭhira as the legal heir to Pāṇḍu’s realm and calls for him to govern with the elders' approval.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra explains succession rules using historical examples.
chapters.es: Dhṛtarāṣṭra warns Duryodhana by recounting ancestral precedents of succession. He cites King Yayāti, who bypassed his eldest son Yadu for disobedience and installed the youngest, Puru. He describes how the eldest brother Devāpi lost his claim due to a skin defect, known as tvagdoṣa, leading his brother Śāntanu to the throne. Acknowledging his own exclusion from the crown due to blindness, Dhṛtarāṣṭra identifies Yudhiṣṭhira as the rightful heir and commands his son to surrender half the kingdom to maintain peace.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana rejects peace and prepares his army for war.
chapters.es: Duryodhana rejects the counsel of his elders and orders his eleven akṣauhiṇīs to march toward Kurukshetra under the puṣya constellation. With Bhīṣma leading the host, the kings prepare for battle. Kṛṣṇa returns to the Pāṇḍavas and reports the failure of diplomacy. He describes his attempts at sāma and bheda, his display of non-human deeds, and the refusal to grant even five villages. Since conciliation failed, Kṛṣṇa declares that only daṇḍa, or force, remains to resolve the conflict.

chapters.subtitle: The Pandavas choose leaders and march to Kurukṣetra.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira organizes seven akṣauhiṇīs for the coming war. His brothers propose various commanders, including Virāṭa and Drupada, but Arjuna highlights Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍī as the ones capable of facing Bhīṣma. Deferring to Kṛṣṇa, the army marches to Kurukṣetra amidst the blaring of the pāñcajanya conch. They establish a fortified camp along the Hiraṇvatī river. Yudhiṣṭhira stocks the camp with physicians, heaps of weapons, and supplies while allied kings arrive to join the Pandava cause.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana orders his army to prepare for war.
chapters.es: Duryodhana commands Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni to prepare for battle following Kṛṣṇa’s failed peace mission. He orders the construction of fortified camps at Kurukṣetra, ensuring they are stocked with water, fuel, and weapons. Warriors rise from their thrones, donning golden armor and tightening their turbans. Charioteers, cavalry, and elephant riders ready their mounts. The city teems with activity like a rising ocean, filled with the sounds of conchs and drums as the troops prepare for their morning march to the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: Yudhiṣṭhira prepares his army for battle after peace fails.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira asks Kṛṣṇa for a report on the failed peace mission. Kṛṣṇa explains that Duryodhana rejected the counsel of Bhīṣma and Vidura, preferring the advice of Karṇa and Śakuni. After hearing that Duryodhana even attempted to imprison Kṛṣṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira orders his commanders to mobilize the army. Although he laments the slaughter of kinsmen, Arjuna reminds him of Kuntī’s earlier instructions to fight. The Pāṇḍavas accept the necessity of war and rest for the night.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana organizes his army and appoints commanders.
chapters.es: At daybreak, Duryodhana organizes eleven akṣauhiṇī divisions. Warriors stock chariots with quivers, spears, and ropes, while others prepare jars of snakes and boiling oil. Seven men mount each elephant, carrying bows and swords. Cavalry units and foot soldiers wearing golden garlands fill the ranks. Duryodhana establishes the hierarchy of units from the patti to the full akṣauhiṇī. He then appoints leaders like Kṛpa, Droṇa, and Karṇa to command these massive forces, ensuring every soldier follows his signals for the coming battle.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana appoints Bhishma as the commander of his army.
chapters.es: Duryodhana asks Bhīṣma to lead the Kaurava army, comparing him to the mountain Meru. Bhīṣma accepts the post of senāpati but vows to spare the Pāṇḍava brothers while killing ten thousand warriors daily. Karṇa refuses to fight as long as Bhīṣma remains in command. After a formal consecration marked by drums and conches, blood rain falls and the earth shakes. The army marches to Kurukṣetra and establishes a camp modeled after the city of Hāstinapura.

chapters.subtitle: Yudhiṣṭhira chooses his generals and Balarāma leaves for pilgrimage.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira appoints seven commanders for his divisions, including Drupada, Virāṭa, and Śikhaṇḍin. He names Dhṛṣṭadyumna as the supreme general and Arjuna as the leader of all, with Kṛṣṇa acting as charioteer. Balarāma arrives in the assembly clad in blue silk. He declares his neutral affection for both Bhīma and Duryodhana, his pupils in mace-fighting. Unable to witness the impending slaughter, he refuses to join the war and departs for a pilgrimage along the Sarasvatī river.

chapters.subtitle: Rukmī offers help to both sides and is rejected.
chapters.es: Rukmī arrives at the Pāṇḍava camp carrying the divine vijaya bow. He offers military assistance to Arjuna, claiming no warrior matches his strength. Arjuna laughs and rejects the offer, recalling his solitary victories at Khāṇḍava and Virāṭa while wielding the gāṇḍīva. When Duryodhana also dismisses the king’s boastful terms, Rukmī withdraws his army. He and Balarāma remain the only two neutral sovereigns who do not participate in the war.

chapters.subtitle: Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya discuss the start of the war.
chapters.es: Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya for an account of the armies at Kurukshetra. He admits his failure to restrain Duryodhana and laments that human effort fails against diṣṭa. Sanjaya warns the king not to blame his son alone, as individuals suffer for their own misdeeds. He compares humans to dāruyantravat, or wooden puppets, driven by divine will, chance, or past karman. Dhritarashtra prepares to hear the report of the slaughter involving horses, elephants, and kings.

chapters.subtitle: Duryodhana sends a messenger to challenge the Pandavas.
chapters.es: Duryodhana summons Ulūka to deliver a formal challenge to the Pāṇḍavas. He instructs the messenger to recount the loss of the kingdom, the years of forest exile, and the public humiliation of Draupadī. The message demands that Arjuna display his skill with weapons and that Bhīmasena fulfill his vow to drink the blood of Duḥśāsana. Duryodhana declares that the field of Kurukṣetra is prepared and the warriors are ready. He dares them to fight alongside Kṛṣṇa at daybreak.

chapters.subtitle: Ulūka delivers Duryodhana's message and challenges the Pāṇḍavas.
chapters.es: Ulūka enters the Pāṇḍava camp to deliver Duryodhana’s provocation. Standing before Yudhiṣṭhira and Kṛṣṇa, he recounts the humiliation of Draupadī in the assembly and the years of exile. He mocks Bhīma’s service as a cook and Arjuna’s disguise as a eunuch, dismissing their vows as empty words. Duryodhana’s message describes the Kuru host as an uncrossable ocean guarded by Bhīṣma and Droṇa. He rejects the peaceful return of the kingdom, challenging the brothers to prove their worth on the plains of Kurukṣetra.

chapters.subtitle: Kṛṣṇa sends a final warning back to Duryodhana.
chapters.es: Ulūka delivers Duryodhana’s final provocations, incensing the Pāṇḍavas. Bhīmasena glares at Kṛṣṇa with bloodshot eyes, hissing like a serpent. Smiling, Kṛṣṇa tells the messenger to warn Suyodhana to show his manhood tomorrow. He dismisses the idea that his role as a driver renders him powerless, stating he could burn the Kuru host like dry grass. He declares that Arjuna’s chariot will confront the King at dawn and confirms Bhīmasena will drink the blood of Duḥśāsana as vowed.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna vows to strike Bhīṣma as the armies mobilize.
chapters.es: Arjuna looks toward Keśava and responds to the messenger with a vow to strike down Bhīṣma first. He denounces Duryodhana for hiding behind the strength of others while pushing the elderly kinsman toward death. At sunrise, Arjuna promises to fell the grandfather from his chariot with arrows. The messenger Ulūka returns to deliver this defiance, prompting Duryodhana and Karṇa to mobilize their forces. Messengers on camels and swift horses race through the camps, ordering the entire army to prepare for battle before dawn.

chapters.subtitle: Pandava leaders assign warriors to their specific opponents.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira commands the four-fold army of infantry, elephants, chariots, and cavalry to advance. Dhṛṣṭadyumna leads the massive force and assigns specific warriors to their rivals. He positions Śikhaṇḍin against Bhīṣma, Arjuna against Karṇa, and Bhīma against Duryodhana. Younger heroes like Abhimanyu and the sons of Draupadī receive their targets, while Dhṛṣṭadyumna himself prepares to face Droṇa. The commander organizes these units into a vyūha and stands ready for the impending battle.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma evaluates the major warriors of the Kaurava army.
chapters.es: Bhishma accepts command of the Kaurava forces after bowing to the spear-wielding deity Kumāra. He promises to deploy divine and human vyūha formations to confuse the Pandavas. At Duryodhana’s request, Bhishma begins classifying the army's leaders. He identifies the Kuru brothers as masters of the mace and sword trained by Droṇa. He labels Kṛtavarman and Śalya as atiratha combatants and highlights Jayadratha’s status as a double-chariot warrior driven by his previous humiliation during the abduction of Draupadī.

chapters.subtitle: Warriors and leaders join the Kaurava army for war.
chapters.es: Sudakṣiṇa leads the Kāmboja army as it descends like a swarm of locusts. Nīla of Māhiṣmatī dons blue armor to seek revenge against Sahadeva. Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti strike with maces and spears, while the five Trigarta brothers churn the enemy forces like crocodiles in the Gaṅgā. The young princes Lakṣmaṇa and the son of Duḥśāsana join the chariot ranks. Kṛpa, compared to the warrior Kārttikeya, moves through the opposing army like fire, wielding diverse bows and weapons.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma evaluates the strengths of the Kaurava army leaders.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma identifies the roles and fighting styles of the Kaurava warriors. Śakuni leads fast troops with unusual weapons. Aśvatthāman possesses celestial arms and divine power, yet his attachment to life complicates his ranking. The aged Droṇa prepares to scatter the Pāṇḍava forces like wind-blown fire, despite his affection for Arjuna. Bāhlīka fights as an atiratha who never retreats from the field. Bhagadatta, an expert in elephant warfare, brings experience from previous encounters with the wielder of the gāṇḍīva bow.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma insults Karna, who vows not to fight.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma evaluates the Gāndhāra princes Acala and Vṛṣaka as capable warriors before turning to Karṇa. He classifies Karṇa as an ardharatha, a half-charioteer, citing the loss of his innate armor and earrings alongside the curses of Paraśurāma and a Brahmin. Droṇa supports this assessment, noting Karṇa’s tendency toward recklessness. Angered by this public slight, Karṇa accuses Bhīṣma of weakening the army’s morale through personal malice. He vows not to fight for Duryodhana until Bhīṣma has fallen on the battlefield.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma lists the fighting ranks of the Pāṇḍava brothers.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma rebukes Karṇa by recalling his victory over kings at Kāśī. Duryodhana asks for a classification of the enemy’s strengths before the morning battle. Bhīṣma describes Yudhiṣṭhira as a ratha and Bhīmasena as possessing the power of ten thousand elephants. He warns that the brothers, seeking revenge for Draupadī, fight like lions. Only Bhīṣma and Droṇa can withstand Arjuna, who wields the Gāṇḍīva and divine weapons on a chariot driven by Vāsudeva.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma lists the great warriors fighting for the Pandavas.
chapters.es: Abhimanyu leads the Pandava forces as a rathayūthapayūthapa, matching the skill of Arjuna and Krishna. Alongside him, the five sons of Draupadi and Uttara serve as chariot-warriors. Satyaki and the brothers Yudhamanyu and Uttamaujas bring thousands of cavalry and elephants to the field. Though advanced in years, Virata and Drupada command their own akṣauhiṇī units. Bound by kinship and bhakti, these veterans and young heroes prepare to strike the Kuru ranks like fire and wind.

chapters.subtitle: The Pandava army's commanders and their ranks are described.
chapters.es: Śikhaṇḍī leads the chariot-line to support Arjuna while the commander Dhṛṣṭadyumna prepares his divisions with the force of an angry Pinākī. The youth Kṣatradharma ranks as an ardharatha, yet kings like Dhṛṣṭaketu and the five Kekaya brothers bring vast, red-bannered forces to the field. Senior leaders, including the Pāṇḍya ruler and Vasudāna, hold the status of atiratha. These warriors and their allies, such as Cekitāna and the Pāñcāla princes, assemble a host that resembles the rising ocean.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma identifies enemy warriors and vows to spare Śikhaṇḍin.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma names the Pāṇḍava commanders, identifying Kuntibhoja as an atiratha and Ghaṭotkaca as a master of māyā. He prepares to confront Arjuna and Vāsudeva, comparing their appearance to the sun and moon. Recalling his renunciation of the throne and his brahmacarya vow, Bhīṣma refuses to strike Śikhaṇḍin. Because Śikhaṇḍin was born female, Bhīṣma adheres to his code against fighting women. He pledges to engage the opposing kings but vows he will not kill the sons of Kuntī or the female-born Śikhaṇḍin.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma explains how he abducted the three princesses of Kashi.
chapters.es: Bhishma explains his refusal to strike Śikhaṇḍin by recounting the abduction of the princesses of Kāśī. Following the death of Śantanu, Bhishma installed his younger brothers on the throne of Hastinapura. To secure wives for Vicitravīrya, he traveled to a svayaṃvara and seized Ambā, Ambikā, and Ambālikā. He repelled the pursuing kings with a rain of arrows, toppling their banners and horses. After defeating the host, he presented the three sisters to Satyavatī as a prize of valor or vīryaśulka.

chapters.subtitle: Ambā asks Bhīṣma to let her marry King Śālva.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma presents the three princesses of Kāśī to Satyavatī as brides for his brother. Satyavatī accepts them, but the eldest daughter, Ambā, halts the marriage ceremony to speak privately with Bhīṣma. She explains that she has already chosen King Śālva as her husband in secret. Appealing to Bhīṣma’s devotion to dharma and his famous vow of truth, she asks for her release. She argues that forcing her into this union violates proper conduct since her mind remains fixed on another.

chapters.subtitle: King Śālva refuses to marry the princess Ambā.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma releases the princess Ambā, who travels to King Śālva’s city under the protection of elders. She requests that Śālva accept her as his wife, but he refuses. He claims that Bhīṣma’s victory in battle made her another man’s property. Ambā swears her loyalty, yet Śālva discards her like a snake shedding its old skin. Bound by fear of Bhīṣma, the king ignores her weeping and sends her away. Ambā leaves the city alone, crying like a kurarī bird.

chapters.subtitle: Amba seeks refuge with ascetics after being rejected.
chapters.es: Amba departs the city, isolated by her family and rejected by King Śālva. She identifies Bhīṣma as the origin of her grief and contemplates his defeat through tapas or war. Reaching a forest retreat, she describes her abduction and abandonment to the dwelling ascetics. She asks to enter a life of penance, viewing her plight as the fruit of past actions. The sage Śaikhavatya and the community of hermits offer her refuge and promise to assist her.

chapters.subtitle: Amba meets her grandfather and seeks help from Rāma.
chapters.es: Ascetics debate the fate of the rejected princess as she lingers in the forest. They urge her to return to her father’s palace, but she refuses to face the judgment of her kin. Her maternal grandfather, the royal sage Hotravāhana, arrives and hears her account. He discourages her from a life of solitary penance and advises her to seek Rāma Jāmadagnya. He promises that the warrior-sage will either restore her status or confront Bhīṣma in battle.

chapters.subtitle: Hotravāhana recounts Ambā's abduction and rejection to Akṛtavraṇa.
chapters.es: King Hotravāhana advises his granddaughter Ambā to seek the warrior-sage Rāma Jāmadagnya on Mahendra mountain. When Rāma’s follower Akṛtavraṇa arrives, the king recounts how Bhīṣma abducted Ambā from her svayaṃvara and later released her to King Śālva. Rejected by Śālva due to suspicion, Ambā refuses to return home out of shame. She blames Bhīṣma for her misfortune and waits in the forest to ask Rāma for aid, hoping his intervention will resolve her grief and restore her honor.

chapters.subtitle: Amba asks Rama Jamadagnya to kill Bhishma for her.
chapters.es: Amba explains how Bhishma’s abduction led to Śālva’s rejection. Rāma Jāmadagnya arrives at the hermitage bearing a bow and a paraśvadha. Amba bows at his feet and recounts her distress, identifying Bhishma’s actions as the source of her ruin. While Rāma offers to mediate with King Śālva, Amba insists that the Kuru elder is responsible for her plight. She requests the warrior-sage to kill Bhishma in battle, seeking vengeance against the man who forcibly seized her from her home.

chapters.subtitle: Rāma agrees to confront Bhīṣma on Ambā’s behalf.
chapters.es: Ambā repeatedly asks Rāma to slay Bhīṣma. Initially reluctant to take up arms except for the sake of brāhmaṇas, Rāma offers to reconcile the dispute through words. The sage Akṛtavraṇa reminds him of his vow to protect those seeking refuge and to challenge arrogant kṣatriyas. Rāma resolves to confront Bhīṣma. He vows to kill the Kuru hero if his command is ignored. Accompanied by Ambā and several ascetics, Rāma travels to Kurukṣetra and camps along the banks of the Sarasvatī river.

chapters.subtitle: Parashurama orders Bhishma to marry Amba, leading to war.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma greets Jamadagnya at the kingdom’s edge with ritual offerings. The sage commands him to marry the princess of Kāśī, arguing that Bhīṣma ruined her marriage prospects. Bhīṣma refuses, citing his lifelong vow and the woman’s preference for Śālva. As the teacher threatens violence, Bhīṣma invokes the right to resist a guru who has abandoned the proper path. He rejects the demand to house a woman who loves another and challenges his preceptor to a duel at Kurukṣetra.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma and Parashurama prepare for battle at Kurukṣetra.
chapters.es: Rāma challenges Bhishma to meet him at Kurukṣetra for a duel to the death. Bhishma equips a silver chariot drawn by white horses and dons white armor, a white uṣṇīṣa, and a white ātapatra. After receiving his mother’s blessing, he travels to the battlefield and blows his śaṅkha. The river goddess Gaṅgā appears in person to plead with both her son and his former teacher to abandon the fight. Both warriors refuse her requests, and the gathered sages prepare to witness the combat.

chapters.subtitle: Bhishma and Parashurama begin their battle.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma refuses to fight Paraśurāma on foot. The sage claims the earth as his chariot and the Vedas as his horses, then manifests a celestial vehicle. After receiving his guru's blessing, Bhīṣma returns to his chariot. He avoids striking the sage’s brāhmaṇa nature, aiming only at his weapons. His arrows cause Paraśurāma to bleed like a flowering aśoka tree. Though he breaks the sage’s bow, Bhīṣma feels remorse for wounding his teacher. The battle ends at sunset.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma and Rāma exchange arrows and celestial weapons.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma salutes his teacher before the duel resumes at sunrise. They exchange snake-like arrows and counter celestial astras, meeting the Vāyavya with the Guhyaka and the Āgneya with the Vāruṇa. After a blow to the chest, Bhīṣma’s charioteer withdraws him briefly. Returning, Bhīṣma strikes Rāma, who faints and is revived by water and blessings. The sky fills with missiles that obscure the sun, igniting from friction and falling as ash. Rāma kills Bhīṣma's horses before the combat ends at dusk.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma and Paraśurāma fight with divine weapons until sunset.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma and Rāma exchange divine weapons in a continuous duel. Rāma hurls a flaming śakti, which Bhīṣma strikes down in three pieces. When Rāma launches twelve spears resembling suns, Bhīṣma counters them with a net of arrows. Rāma’s subsequent shower of shafts damages Bhīṣma's chariot and axle, yet Bhīṣma retaliates until Rāma bleeds from his wounds. Both combatants remain heavily pierced by arrows as the sun sets behind the mountains, bringing the day’s conflict to a close.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma and Rāma Jamadagnya wound each other in battle.
chapters.es: At sunrise, Rāma Jamadagnya kills the charioteer and strikes his opponent’s chest. Eight brāhmaṇas catch the falling warrior before he touches the earth, while the river Gaṅgā holds the reins of his horses. Revived, he returns to the chariot and pierces Rāma’s heart. As Rāma collapses, blood rains from the sky and an eclipse darkens the sun. Vultures and jackals cry out until sunset ends the day’s combat. This duel persists for twenty-three days.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma receives a divine weapon in a dream.
chapters.es: Wounded by arrows and weary from battle, Bhīṣma prays for a sign during the night. Eight luminous figures appear in his dream, identifying themselves as his protectors. They reveal the prasvāpa weapon, a power from his previous birth that causes sleep rather than death. The figures instruct him to use this weapon against Paraśurāma and then restore him with the saṃbodhana mantra. By putting his preceptor to sleep, Bhīṣma avoids the sin of killing while ensuring victory.

chapters.subtitle: Bhīṣma and Paraśurāma use powerful weapons against each other.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma and Paraśurāma resume their duel with volleys of arrows. A spear strikes Bhīṣma’s shoulder, drawing blood like red minerals from a mountain. Bhīṣma retaliates, hitting Paraśurāma’s forehead before falling from a deep chest wound. Upon recovering, he forces Paraśurāma to invoke the brāhma weapon. Bhīṣma counters with his own, causing the sky to blaze and the earth to shake. As the world suffers from the heat, Bhīṣma prepares the prasvāpa weapon to end the conflict.

chapters.subtitle: Gods and ancestors intervene to end the battle.
chapters.es: Bhīṣma prepares the prasvāpa weapon to end the conflict, but Nārada and eight celestial figures command him from the sky to spare his teacher. Bhīṣma withdraws the sleep-inducing dart and readies the brahmāstra instead. Meanwhile, the ancestors of Paraśurāma appear, urging the sage to return to his ascetic duties. They identify Bhīṣma as a vasu whose end is already destined. After Gaṅgā and the sages block the battlefield, both warriors lower their bows and acknowledge each other's strength.

chapters.subtitle: Ambā begins a long penance to destroy Bhīṣma.
chapters.es: Paraśurāma admits his inability to defeat Bhīṣma and advises Ambā to yield. She refuses, vowing instead to destroy the warrior through her own tapas. After years of fasting and standing on one toe near the Yamunā, she travels through various tīrthas. Bhīṣma tracks her progress through spies while his mother, Gaṅgā, unsuccessfully tries to dissuade the princess. Ambā eventually divides her being, becoming both a seasonal river in Vatsabhūmi and an ascetic woman continuing her quest for vengeance.

chapters.subtitle: Ambā receives a boon from Śiva and enters fire.
chapters.es: Seeking Bhīṣma’s death, Ambā performs penance and rejects her identity as a woman. Śiva appears among the ascetics to grant her a boon. He promises that she will take another birth in the family of Drupada as a mahāratha and eventually become a man to slay her enemy. Following this vision, Ambā gathers wood and constructs a funeral pyre near the Yamunā river. She declares her vengeful intent and enters the fire to hasten her rebirth in a new body.

chapters.subtitle: Drupada raises his daughter as a son.
chapters.es: King Drupada performs penance to obtain a child capable of slaying Bhīṣma. Śiva grants a boon, predicting the birth of a daughter who will later become a man. When the queen gives birth to a girl, the royal couple conceals her gender and announces her as a son. They perform all male birth ceremonies and name her Śikhaṇḍī. Trusting the divine word, Drupada maintains this secret while raising the child as a male warrior.

chapters.subtitle: Drupada marries his daughter Śikhaṇḍin to another woman.
chapters.es: King Drupada raises his daughter Śikhaṇḍin as a prince, training her in weaponry under Droṇa. To fulfill a divine promise, the king arranges a marriage with the daughter of King Hiraṇyavarman of Daśārṇa. After the wedding, the bride discovers Śikhaṇḍin is a woman and alerts her attendants. Enraged by the report, Hiraṇyavarman sends a messenger to the Pāñcāla palace. He denounces the union as a fraud and threatens to destroy Drupada and his kin for the insult.

chapters.subtitle: King Hiranyavarma threatens war after learning Shikhandi is female.
chapters.es: King Hiranyavarma mobilizes his army against the Pañcāla kingdom upon learning that Śikhaṇḍī is a woman. He sends a messenger to threaten King Drupada, promising death for the deception regarding the marriage alliance. Overcome by fear, Drupada retreats to his inner chambers to confront his wife. He admits to raising their daughter as a son through masculine saṃskāra rites but now demands the truth to face the invasion. The queen prepares to disclose the facts of her child’s birth to her husband.

chapters.subtitle: Shikhandini asks a forest spirit to become a man.
chapters.es: Śikhaṇḍinī flees to a desolate forest to spare her parents from the King of Daśārṇa’s impending invasion. She enters the white-plastered shrine of the yakṣa Sthūṇākarṇa and begins a fast to end her life. When the spirit appears, Śikhaṇḍinī explains how her false identity threatens her father’s kingdom. She petitions the yakṣa for a physical transformation into a man, seeking to resolve the conflict and protect the city of the Pāñcālas from destruction.

chapters.subtitle: Śikhaṇḍī becomes a man and Bhīṣma refuses to fight.
chapters.es: Śikhaṇḍī exchanges her gender with the Yakṣa Sthūṇa to become a man. King Drupada proves this masculinity to King Hiraṇyavarman through an inspection by maidens. When Kubera finds Sthūṇa in a female form, he curses the Yakṣa to remain so until Śikhaṇḍī dies. Now a male warrior, Śikhaṇḍī masters the dhanurveda under Droṇa. Bhīṣma narrates these events to explain his refusal to fight anyone born as a woman, even if they later acquire a male body.

chapters.subtitle: Kaurava leaders estimate the time to defeat the enemy.
chapters.es: Duryodhana asks his commanders how long they require to annihilate the Pāṇḍava forces. Bhīṣma and Droṇa both claim they can finish the task in one month. Kṛpa estimates two months, while Drauṇi promises ten days. Karṇa asserts he can destroy the entire host in only five days. Hearing this boast, Bhīṣma laughs and reminds Karṇa that he has not yet faced Arjuna and Vāsudeva in battle. The warriors offer these timelines based on their mastery of divyāstra.

chapters.subtitle: Arjuna discusses the time needed to win the war.
chapters.es: Yudhiṣṭhira relays reports from his spies regarding the Kaurava leaders’ claims. Bhīṣma and Droṇa estimate a month to defeat the Pāṇḍava forces, while Karṇa claims five days. When questioned, Arjuna looks toward Kṛṣṇa and asserts he could destroy the world in a moment using the pāśupata weapon received from Śiva. He clarifies that using such weapons against common soldiers is improper. Instead, the Pāṇḍava brothers and their allies will rely on fair combat to achieve victory.

chapters.subtitle: The Kaurava army reaches the battlefield and builds camps.
chapters.es: At daybreak, the kings bathe and perform fire sacrifices before marching toward the Kurukṣetra plains. Dressed in white and adorned with garlands, warriors from across the land, including Śaka and Yavana tribes, assemble behind Duryodhana. They establish a fortified camp on the western border, constructed to resemble the capital city. Duryodhana provides food and resources for the soldiers, artisans, and merchants while clearing a five-yojana circle of land for the impending engagement.

chapters.subtitle: Yudhishthira organizes the Pandava army for the march
chapters.es: Yudhishthira organizes the Pāṇḍava forces into specific divisions for the march. Dhrishtadyumna leads the vanguard, followed by Abhimanyu and the sons of Draupadi. Bhīma commands a division of ten thousand horsemen and two thousand elephants. In the center, Virāṭa and Jayatsena advance alongside Yudhamanyu and Uttamaujas, who guard the path for Vāsudeva and Arjuna. The army moves like the flowing Gaṅgā, accompanied by the clamor of thousands of bherī drums and śaṅkha shells, while Yudhishthira remains with the main body of kings.

data.v: नारायणं नमस्कृत्य नरं चैव नरोत्तमम् । देवीं सरस्वतीं चैव ततो जयमुदीरयेत् ॥
data.es: Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa, to Nara, the best of men, and to Goddess Sarasvatī, one should utter the word 'Jaya'.
data.anv: नारायणम् (च) एव नरोत्तमम् नरम् देवीं सरस्वतीं च नमस्कृत्य ततः जयम् उदीरयेत् ॥

data.v: लोमहर्षणपुत्र उग्रश्रवाः सूतः पौराणिको नैमिषारण्ये शौनकस्य कुलपतेर्द्वादशवार्षिके सत्रे ॥
data.es: Ugraśravas, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa and a reciter of the Purāṇas, was present at the twelve-year sacrifice of the patriarch Śaunaka in the Naimiṣa forest.
data.anv: लोमहर्षण-पुत्रः उग्रश्रवाः सूतः पौराणिकः नैमिष-अरण्ये कुलपतेः शौनकस्य द्वादश-वार्षिके सत्रे (आसीत्) ॥

data.v: समासीनानभ्यगच्छद्ब्रह्मर्षीन्संशितव्रतान् । विनयावनतो भूत्वा कदाचित्सूतनन्दनः ॥
data.es: Once, that son of a Sūta, bowing with humility, approached the assembled Brahmarṣis who were firm in their vows.
data.anv: सूत-नन्दनः कदाचित् विनय-अवनतः भूत्वा समासीनान् संशित-व्रतान् ब्रह्मर्षीन् अभ्यगच्छत् ॥

data.v: तमाश्रममनुप्राप्तं नैमिषारण्यवासिनः । चित्राः श्रोतुं कथास्तत्र परिवव्रुस्तपस्विनः ॥
data.es: Upon his arrival at the hermitage, the ascetics residing in the Naimiṣa forest gathered around him to hear diverse and wonderful stories.
data.anv: तम् आश्रमम् अनुप्राप्तम् (तं दृष्ट्वा) नैमिष-अरण्य-वासिनः तपस्विनः चित्राः कथाः श्रोतुम् तत्र (तम्) परिवव्रुः ॥

data.v: अभिवाद्य मुनींस्तांस्तु सर्वानेव कृताञ्जलिः । अपृच्छत्स तपोवृद्धिं सद्भिश्चैवाभिनन्दितः ॥
data.es: Greeting all those sages with joined palms, he inquired about the progress of their penance and was warmly welcomed by those virtuous ones.
data.anv: सः तान् सर्वान् एव मुनीन् कृताञ्जलिः (सन्) अभिवाद्य तपो-वृद्धिम् अपृच्छत् सद्धिः च एव अभिनन्दितः (अभवत्) ॥

data.v: अथ तेषूपविष्टेषु सर्वेष्वेव तपस्विषु । निर्दिष्टमासनं भेजे विनयाल्लोमहर्षणिः ॥
data.es: Then, after all those ascetics had taken their seats, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa humbly occupied the seat assigned to him.
data.anv: अथ सर्वेषु एव तेषु तपस्विषु उपविष्टेषु लोमहर्षणिः विनयात् निर्दिष्टम् आसनम् भेजे ॥

data.v: सुखासीनं ततस्तं तु विश्रान्तमुपलक्ष्य च । अथापृच्छदृषिस्तत्र कश्चित्प्रस्तावयन्कथाः ॥
data.es: Seeing him comfortably seated and rested, a certain sage there, introducing the conversation, inquired of him.
data.anv: ततः तम् सुख-आसीनम् विश्रान्तम् च उपलक्ष्य अथ तत्र कश्चित् ऋषिः कथाः प्रस्तावयन् अपृच्छत् ॥

data.v: कुत आगम्यते सौते क्व चायं विहृतस्त्वया । कालः कमलपत्राक्ष शंसैतत्पृच्छतो मम ॥
data.es: O lotus-eyed son of a Sūta, from where have you come? Where have you spent your time? Tell this to me as I ask you.
data.anv: कमल-पत्र-अक्ष सौते कुतः आगम्यते क्व च त्वया अयम् कालः विहृतः एतत् पृच्छतः मम शंस ॥

data.v: जनमेजयस्य राजर्षेः सर्पसत्रे महात्मनः । समीपे पार्थिवेन्द्रस्य सम्यक्पारिक्षितस्य च ॥
data.es: I was present at the snake sacrifice of the high-souled royal sage Janamejaya, the lord of kings and the son of Parikṣit.
data.anv: महात्मनः राजर्षेः पार्थिव-इन्द्रस्य पारिक्षितस्य जनमेजयस्य सर्प-सत्रे समीपे (आसम्) ॥

data.v: कृष्णद्वैपायनप्रोक्ताः सुपुण्या विविधाः कथाः । कथिताश्चापि विधिवद्या वैशंपायनेन वै ॥
data.es: There, I heard the various and holy stories composed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, which were duly recited by Vaiśampāyana.
data.anv: (तत्र) कृष्ण-द्वैपायन-प्रोक्ताः विविधाः सुपुण्याः कथाः याः वै वैशम्पायनेन विधिवत् कथिताः (ताः श्रुतवान्) ॥

data.v: श्रुत्वाहं ता विचित्रार्था महाभारतसंश्रिताः । बहूनि संपरिक्रम्य तीर्थान्यायतनानि च ॥
data.es: Having traveled across many holy places and shrines, and having heard those various narratives associated with the Mahābhārata, I have arrived here.
data.anv: अहम् बहूनि तीर्थानि च आयतनानि संपरिक्रम्य महाभारत-संश्रिताः ताः विचित्र-अर्थाः (कथाः) श्रुत्वा (आगतः अस्मि) ।

data.v: समन्तपञ्चकं नाम पुण्यं द्विजनिषेवितम् । गतवानस्मि तं देशं युद्धं यत्राभवत्पुरा । पाण्डवानां कुरूणां च सर्वेषां च महीक्षिताम् ॥
data.es: I have visited that sacred region known as Samantapañcaka, frequented by brāhmaṇas, where the ancient war between the Pāṇḍavas, the Kurus, and all the kings of the earth took place.
data.anv: यत्र पुरा पाण्डवानाम् कुरूणाम् च सर्वेषाम् महीक्षिताम् च युद्धम् अभवत्, द्विज-निषेवितम् पुण्यम् समन्तपञ्चकम् नाम तम् देशम् गतवान् अस्मि ।

data.v: दिदृक्षुरागतस्तस्मात्समीपं भवतामिह । आयुष्मन्तः सर्व एव ब्रह्मभूता हि मे मताः ॥
data.es: Desirous of seeing you, I have come from there to your presence. O long-lived ones, in my opinion, all of you are indeed souls who have realized Brahman.
data.anv: तस्मात् दिदृक्षुः इह भवताम् समीपम् आगतः (अस्मि) । आयुष्मन्तः ! मे मताः सर्वे एव हि ब्रह्म-भूताः ।

data.v: अस्मिन्यज्ञे महाभागाः सूर्यपावकवर्चसः । कृताभिषेकाः शुचयः कृतजप्या हुताग्नयः । भवन्त आसते स्वस्था ब्रवीमि किमहं द्विजाः ॥
data.es: In this sacrifice, you illustrious ones, possessing the radiance of the sun and fire, sit composed, having performed your ablutions, being pure, having completed your chants, and having offered oblations to the fire. O dvijas, what shall I recite?
data.anv: अस्मिन् यज्ञे महाभागाः सूर्य-पावक-वर्चसः कृत-अभिषेकाः शुचयः कृत-जप्याः हुत-अग्नयः स्वस्थाः भवन्तः आसते । हे द्विजाः ! अहम् किम् ब्रवीमि ?

data.v: पुराणसंश्रिताः पुण्याः कथा वा धर्मसंश्रिताः । इतिवृत्तं नरेन्द्राणामृषीणां च महात्मनाम् ॥
data.es: Shall I recite the sacred tales based on the Purāṇas or those concerned with Dharma, or the histories of kings and great-souled ṛṣis?
data.anv: पुराण-संश्रिताः पुण्याः कथाः वा धर्म-संश्रिताः (वा) नरेन्द्राणाम् महात्मनाम् ऋषीणाम् च इतिवृत्तम् (ब्रवीमि) ?

data.v: द्वैपायनेन यत्प्रोक्तं पुराणं परमर्षिणा । सुरैर्ब्रह्मर्षिभिश्चैव श्रुत्वा यदभिपूजितम् ॥
data.es: That ancient lore which was spoken by the great seer Dvaipāyana, and which, upon being heard, was highly honored by the gods and the celestial sages alike.
data.anv: परम-ऋषिणा द्वैपायनेन यत् पुराणम् प्रोक्तम्, सुरैः च एव ब्रह्म-ऋषिभिः श्रुत्वा यद् अभिपूजितम् ।

data.v: तस्याख्यानवरिष्ठस्य विचित्रपदपर्वणः । सूक्ष्मार्थन्याययुक्तस्य वेदार्थैर्भूषितस्य च ॥
data.es: The story of that most excellent of narratives, which possesses wonderful words and chapters, is endowed with subtle meanings and logic, and is adorned with the essence of the Vedas.
data.anv: तस्य विचित्र-पद-पर्वणः सूक्ष्म-अर्थ-न्याय-युक्तस्य वेद-अर्थैः भूषितस्य च आख्यान-वरिष्ठस्य (कथाम्) ।

data.v: भारतस्येतिहासस्य पुण्यां ग्रन्थार्थसंयुताम् । संस्कारोपगतां ब्राह्मीं नानाशास्त्रोपबृंहिताम् ॥
data.es: The sacred collection of the history of the Bhāratas, which is endowed with profound text and meaning, refined in expression, divine in nature, and augmented by various scriptures.
data.anv: भारतस्य इतिहासस्य पुण्याम् ग्रन्थ-अर्थ-संयुताम् संस्कार-उपगताम् ब्राह्मीम् नाना-शास्त्र-उपबृंहिताम् (संहिताम्) ।

data.v: जनमेजयस्य यां राज्ञो वैशंपायन उक्तवान् । यथावत्स ऋषिस्तुष्ट्या सत्रे द्वैपायनाज्ञया ॥
data.es: That which the sage Vaiśampāyana, at the command of Dvaipāyana, correctly recited with gratification to King Janamejaya during the sacrificial session.
data.anv: द्वैपायन-आज्ञया सत्रे तुष्ट्या सः ऋषिः वैशम्पायनः यथावत् राज्ञः जनमेजयस्य याम् उक्तवान् ।

data.v: वेदैश्चतुर्भिः समितां व्यासस्याद्भुतकर्मणः । संहितां श्रोतुमिच्छामो धर्म्यां पापभयापहाम् ॥
data.es: We desire to hear the righteous collection composed by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds, which is equal to the four Vedas and is the destroyer of the fear of sin.
data.anv: अद्भुत-कर्मणः व्यासस्य चतुर्भिः वेदैः समिताम् धर्म्याम् पाप-भय-अपहाम् संहिताम् श्रोतुम् इच्छामः ।

data.v: आद्यं पुरुषमीशानं पुरुहूतं पुरुष्टुतम् । ऋतमेकाक्षरं ब्रह्म व्यक्ताव्यक्तं सनातनम् ॥
data.es: Saluting the primordial, sovereign Puruṣa, who is invoked by many and praised by many; who is Truth, the single-syllabled Brahman, manifest and unmanifest, and eternal.
data.anv: आद्यं ईशानं पुरुहूतं पुरुष्टुतम् ऋतम् एकाक्षरं ब्रह्म व्यक्ताव्यक्तं सनातनं पुरुषं (नमस्कृत्य)

data.v: असच्च सच्चैव च यद्विश्वं सदसतः परम् । परावराणां स्रष्टारं पुराणं परमव्ययम् ॥
data.es: Saluting Him who is both the cause and the effect, who is the universe and yet beyond existence and non-existence; the ancient, supreme, and inexhaustible creator of the high and the low.
data.anv: यत् असत् च सत् च एव (अस्ति) यत् विश्वं सदसतः परं परावराणां स्रष्टारं पुराणं परमं अव्ययम् (तम् पुरुषं नमस्कृत्य)

data.v: मङ्गल्यं मङ्गलं विष्णुं वरेण्यमनघं शुचिम् । नमस्कृत्य हृषीकेशं चराचरगुरुं हरिम् ॥
data.es: Having offered salutations to Viṣṇu, the auspiciousness of all auspiciousness, the preeminent, sinless, and pure Lord of the senses, who is Hari, the preceptor of all things moving and motionless.
data.anv: मङ्गल्यं मङ्गलं वरेण्यं अनघं शुचिं चराचरगुरुं विष्णुं हृषीकेशं हरिं नमस्कृत्य

data.v: महर्षेः पूजितस्येह सर्वलोके महात्मनः । प्रवक्ष्यामि मतं कृत्स्नं व्यासस्यामिततेजसः ॥
data.es: I shall now fully proclaim the thought and composition of the great sage Vyāsa, who is worshipped in all worlds, possessed of boundless luster and a great soul.
data.anv: इह सर्वलोके पूजितस्य महात्मनः अमिततेजसः महर्षेः व्यासस्य कृत्स्नं मतं प्रवक्ष्यामि

data.v: आचख्युः कवयः केचित्संप्रत्याचक्षते परे । आख्यास्यन्ति तथैवान्ये इतिहासमिमं भुवि ॥
data.es: Some poets have already narrated this history, others are relating it now, and likewise, others shall proclaim it upon this earth in the future.
data.anv: केचित् कवयः इमम् इतिहासम् आचख्युः परे संप्रति आचक्षते तथा एव अन्ये भुवि आख्यास्यन्ति

data.v: इदं तु त्रिषु लोकेषु महज्ज्ञानं प्रतिष्ठितम् । विस्तरैश्च समासैश्च धार्यते यद्द्विजातिभिः ॥
data.es: This great knowledge is established across the three worlds, preserved by the twice-born in both detailed and abridged forms.
data.anv: इदं तु महत् ज्ञानं त्रिषु लोकेषु प्रतिष्ठितम् यत् द्विजातिभिः विस्तरैः च समासैः च धार्यते

data.v: अलंकृतं शुभैः शब्दैः समयैर्दिव्यमानुषैः । छन्दोवृत्तैश्च विविधैरन्वितं विदुषां प्रियम् ॥
data.es: Adorned with elegant words and divine as well as human conventions, this work is composed in various poetic meters and is dear to the learned.
data.anv: शुभैः शब्दैः अलंकृतं दिव्यमानुषैः समयैः विविधैः छन्दोवृत्तैः च अन्वितं विदुषां प्रियम् (इदं ज्ञानं वर्तते)

data.v: निष्प्रभेऽस्मिन्निरालोके सर्वतस्तमसावृते । बृहदण्डमभूदेकं प्रजानां बीजमक्षयम् ॥
data.es: In this darkness, void of light and enveloped on all sides by gloom, there arose a single, imperishable, mighty egg, the seed of all creatures.
data.anv: अस्मिन् निष्प्रभे निरालोके सर्वतः तमसा आवृते (सति) प्रजानां बीजं अक्षयं एकं बृहत् अण्डम् अभूत्

data.v: युगस्यादौ निमित्तं तन्महद्दिव्यं प्रचक्षते । यस्मिंस्तच्छ्रूयते सत्यं ज्योतिर्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥
data.es: At the beginning of the Yuga, that egg is called the great divine cause, within which is heard of the true, eternal light, the Brahman.
data.anv: युगस्य आदौ तत् महत् दिव्यं निमित्तं प्रचक्षते यस्मिन् तत् सत्यं सनातनं ज्योतिः ब्रह्म श्रूयते

data.v: अद्भुतं चाप्यचिन्त्यं च सर्वत्र समतां गतम् । अव्यक्तं कारणं सूक्ष्मं यत्तत्सदसदात्मकम् ॥
data.es: That Brahman is wonderful, inconceivable, omnipresent, and equanimous; it is the unmanifest, subtle cause characterized by both being and non-being.
data.anv: यत् तत् अद्भुतं च अपि अचिन्त्यं च सर्वत्र समतां गतम् अव्यक्तं सूक्ष्मं कारणं सदसदात्मकम् (ब्रह्म अस्ति)

data.v: यस्मात्पितामहो जज्ञे प्रभुरेकः प्रजापतिः । ब्रह्मा सुरगुरुः स्थाणुर्मनुः कः परमेष्ठ्यथ ॥
data.es: From whom was born the one Lord, the Grandfather Brahmā, the preceptor of the gods, Sthāṇu, Manu, Ka, and Parameṣṭhin.
data.anv: यस्मात् (एकः) प्रभुः पितामहः (ब्रह्मा) जज्ञे, (सः) सुरगुरुः स्थाणुः मनुः कः परमेष्ठी अथ (अस्ति) ।

data.v: प्राचेतसस्तथा दक्षो दक्षपुत्राश्च सप्त ये । ततः प्रजानां पतयः प्राभवन्नेकविंशतिः ॥
data.es: Likewise, Prācetasa Dakṣa and his seven sons were born; from them arose the twenty-one lords of creatures.
data.anv: तथा प्राचेतसः दक्षः ये च सप्त दक्षपुत्राः (सन्ति), ततः एकविंशतिः प्रजानां पतयः प्राभवन् ।

data.v: पुरुषश्चाप्रमेयात्मा यं सर्वमृषयो विदुः । विश्वेदेवास्तथादित्या वसवोऽथाश्विनावपि ॥
data.es: The Puruṣa of immeasurable soul, whom all seers know, as well as the Viśvedevas, Ādityas, Vasus, and the two Aśvins also appeared.
data.anv: अप्रमेयात्मा पुरुषः च यं सर्वे ऋषयः विदुः, तथा विश्वेदेवाः आदित्याः वसवः अथ अश्विनौ अपि (प्राभवन्) ।

data.v: यक्षाः साध्याः पिशाचाश्च गुह्यकाः पितरस्तथा । ततः प्रसूता विद्वांसः शिष्टा ब्रह्मर्षयोऽमलाः ॥
data.es: The Yakṣas, Sādhyas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and the Pitṛs were produced, followed by the wise, disciplined, and stainless Brahmarṣis.
data.anv: यक्षाः साध्याः पिशाचाः च गुह्यकाः तथा पितरः, ततः विद्वांसः शिष्टाः अमलाः ब्रह्मर्षयः प्रसूताः ।

data.v: राजर्षयश्च बहवः सर्वैः समुदिता गुणैः । आपो द्यौः पृथिवी वायुरन्तरिक्षं दिशस्तथा ॥
data.es: Numerous Rājarṣis endowed with all virtues, along with water, heaven, earth, air, space, and the cardinal directions also manifested.
data.anv: सर्वैः गुणैः समुदिताः बहवः राजर्षयः च, आपः द्यौः पृथिवी वायुः अन्तरिक्षं तथा दिशः (संभूताः) ।

data.v: संवत्सरर्तवो मासाः पक्षाहोरात्रयः क्रमात् । यच्चान्यदपि तत्सर्वं संभूतं लोकसाक्षिकम् ॥
data.es: The years, seasons, months, fortnights, days and nights in succession, and whatever else exists that witnesses the world, all came into being.
data.anv: संवत्सर-ऋतवः मासाः पक्ष-अहोरात्रयः क्रमात्, यत् च अन्यत् अपि तत् सर्वं लोकसाक्षिकं संभूतम् ।

data.v: यदिदं दृश्यते किंचिद्भूतं स्थावरजङ्गमम् । पुनः संक्षिप्यते सर्वं जगत्प्राप्ते युगक्षये ॥
data.es: Whatever mobile or immobile beings are seen here, this entire world is again withdrawn when the end of the Yuga arrives.
data.anv: यत् इदं किंचित् स्थावर-जङ्गमं भूतं दृश्यते, युगक्षये प्राप्ते (सति) तत् सर्वं जगत् पुनः संक्षिप्यते ।

data.v: यथर्तावृतुलिङ्गानि नानारूपाणि पर्यये । दृश्यन्ते तानि तान्येव तथा भावा युगादिषु ॥
data.es: Just as various signs of the seasons appear again and again as the seasons rotate, so do all beings reappear at the beginning of the Yugas.
data.anv: यथा ऋतौ पर्यये नाना-रूपाणि ऋतु-लिङ्गानि तानि तानि एव दृश्यन्ते, तथा युगादिषु भावाः (दृश्यन्ते) ।

data.v: एवमेतदनाद्यन्तं भूतसंहारकारकम् । अनादिनिधनं लोके चक्रं संपरिवर्तते ॥
data.es: Thus, this wheel of time, without beginning or end, which brings about the destruction of beings and is itself eternal, revolves in the world.
data.anv: एवम् एतत् अनादि-अन्तं भूत-संहार-कारकं अनादि-निधनं चक्रं लोके संपरिवर्तते ।

data.v: त्रयस्त्रिंशत्सहस्राणि त्रयस्त्रिंशच्छतानि च । त्रयस्त्रिंशच्च देवानां सृष्टिः संक्षेपलक्षणा ॥
data.es: Thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred, and thirty-three deities constitute this creation described in brief.
data.anv: त्रयस्त्रिंशत् सहस्राणि त्रयस्त्रिंशत् शतानि च त्रयस्त्रिंशत् च देवानां (इति एषा) संक्षेप-लक्षणा सृष्टिः (अस्ति) ।

data.v: दिवस्पुत्रो बृहद्भानुश्चक्षुरात्मा विभावसुः । सविता च ऋचीकोऽर्को भानुराशावहो रविः ॥
data.es: The sons of Dyaus are Bṛhadbhānu, Cakṣus, Ātmā, Vibhāvasu, Savitṛ, Ṛcīka, Arka, Bhānu, Āśāvaha, and Ravi.
data.anv: दिवः पुत्रः बृहद्भानुः चक्षुः आत्मा विभावसुः सविता च ऋचीकः अर्कः भानुः आशावहः रविः (भवन्ति) ।

data.v: पुत्रा विवस्वतः सर्वे मह्यस्तेषां तथावरः । देवभ्राट्तनयस्तस्य तस्मात्सुभ्राडिति स्मृतः ॥
data.es: All these are the sons of Vivasvat. Among them, Mahya was the youngest, whose son was Devabhrāṭ, and from him was born Subhrāṭ.
data.anv: सर्वे विवस्वतः पुत्राः (सन्ति) । तेषाम् अवरः मह्यः तथा तस्य तनयः देवभ्राट् (अस्ति) । तस्मात् सुभ्राट् इति स्मृतः (अस्ति) ।

data.v: सुभ्राजस्तु त्रयः पुत्राः प्रजावन्तो बहुश्रुताः । दशज्योतिः शतज्योतिः सहस्रज्योतिरात्मवान् ॥
data.es: Subhrāṭ had three sons who were prolific, deeply learned, and self-controlled: Daśajyotis, Śatajyotis, and Sahasrajyotis.
data.anv: सुभ्राजः तु प्रजावन्तः बहुश्रुताः आत्मवान् दशज्योतिः शतज्योतिः सहस्रज्योतिः (इति) त्रयः पुत्राः (आसन्) ।

data.v: दश पुत्रसहस्राणि दशज्योतेर्महात्मनः । ततो दशगुणाश्चान्ये शतज्योतेरिहात्मजाः ॥
data.es: The high-souled Daśajyotis had ten thousand sons; Śatajyotis had ten times as many offspring as him.
data.anv: महात्मनः दशज्योतेः दश पुत्रसहस्राणि (आसन्) । ततः इह शतज्योतेः अन्ये दशगुणाः आत्मजाः (आसन्) ।

data.v: भूयस्ततो दशगुणाः सहस्रज्योतिषः सुताः । तेभ्योऽयं कुरुवंशश्च यदूनां भरतस्य च ॥
data.es: Sahasrajyotis had ten times more sons than the former. From them descended the lineage of Kuru, the Yadus, and Bharata.
data.anv: ततः भूयः दशगुणाः सहस्रज्योतिषः सुताः (आसन्) । तेभ्यः अयम् कुरुवंशः च यदूनां भरतस्य च (वंशः जातः) ।

data.v: ययातीक्ष्वाकुवंशश्च राजर्षीणां च सर्वशः । संभूता बहवो वंशा भूतसर्गाः सविस्तराः ॥
data.es: The dynasties of Yayāti and Ikṣvāku, along with numerous lineages of royal sages and the detailed creation of beings, originated from them.
data.anv: ययाति-इक्ष्वाकु-वंशः च सर्वशः राजर्षीणां च बहवः वंशाः सविस्तराः भूतसर्गाः संभूताः ।

data.v: भूतस्थानानि सर्वाणि रहस्यं त्रिविधं च यत् । वेदयोगं सविज्ञानं धर्मोऽर्थः काम एव च ॥
data.es: All habitats of beings, the threefold mystery, Vedic yoga accompanied by knowledge, and the pursuits of Dharma, Artha, and Kāma are described here.
data.anv: सर्वाणि भूतस्थानानि यत् च त्रिविधं रहस्यम् सविज्ञानं वेदयोगं धर्मः अर्थः कामः एव च (अत्र वर्णितम्) ।

data.v: धर्मकामार्थशास्त्राणि शास्त्राणि विविधानि च । लोकयात्राविधानं च संभूतं दृष्टवानृषिः ॥
data.es: The sage beheld the treatises on Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, various other sciences, and the rules for the conduct of worldly affairs, all manifested together.
data.anv: धर्म-काम-अर्थ-शास्त्राणि विविधानि शास्त्राणि च लोकयात्रा-विधानं च ऋषिः संभूतं दृष्टवान् ।

data.v: इतिहासाः सवैयाख्या विविधाः श्रुतयोऽपि च । इह सर्वमनुक्रान्तमुक्तं ग्रन्थस्य लक्षणम् ॥
data.es: Histories with their commentaries and various Vedic scriptures are included. Everything has been enumerated here as the characteristic features of this work.
data.anv: सवैयाख्याः इतिहासाः विविधाः श्रुतयः अपि च (सन्ति) । इह सर्वम् अनुक्रान्तं ग्रन्थस्य लक्षणम् उक्तम् ।

data.v: विस्तीर्यैतन्महज्ज्ञानमृषिः संक्षेपमब्रवीत् । इष्टं हि विदुषां लोके समासव्यासधारणम् ॥
data.es: Having expanded this great knowledge, the sage then related it in brief; for in this world, the learned desire both concise and detailed presentations.
data.anv: एतत् महत् ज्ञानं विस्तीर्य ऋषिः संक्षेपम् अब्रवीत् । हि लोके विदुषाम् समास-व्यास-धारणम् इष्टम् ।

data.v: मन्वादि भारतं केचिदास्तीकादि तथापरे । तथोपरिचराद्यन्ये विप्राः सम्यगधीयते ॥
data.es: Some learned Brāhmaṇas study the Mahābhārata starting from the story of Manu, others from the story of Āstīka, and still others from the story of Uparicara.
data.anv: केचित् मनु-आदि भारतम् (अधीयते), तथा अपरे आस्तीक-आदि (अधीयते), तथा अन्ये विप्राः उपरिचर-आदि सम्यक् अधीयते ।

data.v: विविधं संहिताज्ञानं दीपयन्ति मनीषिणः । व्याख्यातुं कुशलाः केचिद्ग्रन्थं धारयितुं परे ॥
data.es: Wise men illuminate various types of knowledge contained in this collection; some are skilled in explaining the text, while others are proficient in memorizing and retaining it.
data.anv: मनीषिणः विविधं संहिता-ज्ञानं दीपयन्ति, केचित् व्याख्यातुं कुशलाः, परे ग्रन्थं धारयितुं (कुशलाः) ।

data.v: तपसा ब्रह्मचर्येण व्यस्य वेदं सनातनम् । इतिहासमिमं चक्रे पुण्यं सत्यवतीसुतः ॥
data.es: The son of Satyavatī (Vyāsa), having classified the eternal Veda through the power of penance and celibacy, composed this holy history (the Mahābhārata).
data.anv: सत्यवती-सुतः तपसा ब्रह्मचर्येण सनातनम् वेदं व्यस्य इमं पुण्यम् इतिहासम् चक्रे ।

data.v: पराशरात्मजो विद्वान्ब्रह्मर्षिः संशितव्रतः । मातुर्नियोगाद्धर्मात्मा गाङ्गेयस्य च धीमतः ॥
data.es: The learned and righteous sage, the son of Parāśara, a Brahmarṣi of rigid vows, acted upon the command of his mother and the wise Bhīṣma (the son of Gaṅgā).
data.anv: विद्वान् ब्रह्मर्षिः संशित-व्रतः धर्मात्मा पराशर-आत्मजः मातुः धीमतः गाङ्गेयस्य च नियोगात् ।

data.v: क्षेत्रे विचित्रवीर्यस्य कृष्णद्वैपायनः पुरा । त्रीनग्नीनिव कौरव्याञ्जनयामास वीर्यवान् ॥
data.es: In ancient times, the powerful Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana procreated three Kuru princes, who were like the three sacred sacrificial fires, in the lineage of Vicitravīrya.
data.anv: वीर्यवान् कृष्णद्वैपायनः पुरा विचित्रवीर्यस्य क्षेत्रे त्रीन् अग्नीन् इव कौरव्यान जनयामास ।

data.v: उत्पाद्य धृतराष्ट्रं च पाण्डुं विदुरमेव च । जगाम तपसे धीमान्पुनरेवाश्रमं प्रति ॥
data.es: Having fathered Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura, the wise sage returned once again to his hermitage to practice austerities.
data.anv: धीमान् धृतराष्ट्रं पाण्डुं विदुरं च एव उत्पाद्य पुनः एव आश्रमं प्रति तपसे जगाम ।

data.v: तेषु जातेषु वृद्धेषु गतेषु परमां गतिम् । अब्रवीद्भारतं लोके मानुषेऽस्मिन्महानृषिः ॥
data.es: After these princes were born, grew old, and eventually attained the ultimate state (died), the great sage revealed the Mahābhārata to the human world.
data.anv: तेषु जातेषु वृद्धेषु परमां गतिम् गतेषु (सति) महान् ऋषिः अस्मिन् मानुषे लोके भारतम् अब्रवीत् ।

data.v: जनमेजयेन पृष्टः सन्ब्राह्मणैश्च सहस्रशः । शशास शिष्यमासीनं वैशंपायनमन्तिके ॥
data.es: When questioned by King Janamejaya and thousands of Brāhmaṇas, the sage instructed his disciple Vaiśampāyana, who was seated near him.
data.anv: सहस्रशः ब्राह्मणैः च सह जनमेजयेन पृष्टः सन् अन्तिके आसीनं शिष्यं वैशंपायनं शशास ।

data.v: स सदस्यैः सहासीनः श्रावयामास भारतम् । कर्मान्तरेषु यज्ञस्य चोद्यमानः पुनः पुनः ॥
data.es: Seated with the sacrificial assembly and urged repeatedly during the intervals between Vedic rituals, Vaiśampāyana recited the Mahābhārata.
data.anv: सः सदस्यैः सह आसीनः यज्ञस्य कर्म-अन्तरेषु पुनः पुनः चोद्यमानः भारतं श्रावयामास ।

data.v: विस्तरं कुरुवंशस्य गान्धार्या धर्मशीलताम् । क्षत्तुः प्रज्ञां धृतिं कुन्त्याः सम्यग्द्वैपायनोऽब्रवीत् ॥
data.es: Dvaipāyana accurately narrated the expansion of the Kuru dynasty, the religious devotion of Gāndhārī, the wisdom of Vidura (the Kṣattṛ), and the fortitude of Kuntī.
data.anv: द्वैपायनः कुरु-वंशस्य विस्तरं गान्धार्याः धर्म-शीलताम् क्षत्तुः प्रज्ञां कुन्त्याः धृतिं सम्यक् अब्रवीत् ।

data.v: वासुदेवस्य माहात्म्यं पाण्डवानां च सत्यताम् । दुर्वृत्तं धार्तराष्ट्राणामुक्तवान्भगवानृषिः ॥
data.es: The divine sage Vyāsa has described the greatness of Vāsudeva, the truthfulness of the Pāṇḍavas, and the evil conduct of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
data.anv: भगवान् ऋषिः वासुदेवस्य माहात्म्यं पाण्डवानां सत्यताम् च धार्तराष्ट्राणाम् दुर्वृत्तम् (च) उक्तवान् ॥

data.v: चतुर्विंशतिसाहस्रीं चक्रे भारतसंहिताम् । उपाख्यानैर्विना तावद्भारतं प्रोच्यते बुधैः ॥
data.es: He composed the Bhārata collection consisting of twenty-four thousand verses excluding the secondary episodes; only that portion is called the Bhārata by the learned.
data.anv: (सः) उपाख्यानैः विना चतुर्विंशति-साहस्रीं भारत-संहिताम् चक्रे, तावत् बुधैः भारतम् प्रोच्यते ॥

data.v: ततोऽध्यर्धशतं भूयः संक्षेपं कृतवानृषिः । अनुक्रमणिमध्यायं वृत्तान्तानां सपर्वणाम् ॥
data.es: Thereafter, the sage further composed a summary of one hundred and fifty verses as an introductory chapter indexing the events and their respective sections.
data.anv: ततः ऋषिः भूयः स-पर्वणाम् वृत्तान्तानाम् अनुक्रमणिम् अध्यायम् अध्यर्ध-शतम् संक्षेपम् कृतवान् ॥

data.v: इदं द्वैपायनः पूर्वं पुत्रमध्यापयच्छुकम् । ततोऽन्येभ्योऽनुरूपेभ्यः शिष्येभ्यः प्रददौ प्रभुः ॥
data.es: The lord Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana first taught this to his son Śuka, and subsequently imparted it to other worthy disciples.
data.anv: प्रभुः द्वैपायनः इदम् पूर्वम् पुत्रम् शुकम् अध्यापयत्, ततः (सः) अन्येभ्यः अनुरूपेभ्यः शिष्येभ्यः प्रददौ ॥

data.v: नारदोऽश्रावयद्देवानसितो देवलः पितॄन् । गन्धर्वयक्षरक्षांसि श्रावयामास वै शुकः ॥
data.es: Nārada recited it to the gods, Asita-Devala to the ancestors, and Śuka indeed recited it to the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas.
data.anv: नारदः देवान् अश्रावयत्, असितः देवलः पितॄन् (अश्रावयत्), शुकः वै गन्धर्व-यक्ष-रक्षांसि श्रावयामास ॥

data.v: दुर्योधनो मन्युमयो महाद्रुमः; स्कन्धः कर्णः शकुनिस्तस्य शाखाः । दुःशासनः पुष्पफले समृद्धे; मूलं राजा धृतराष्ट्रोऽमनीषी ॥
data.es: Duryodhana is a great tree made of resentment; Karṇa is its trunk, Śakuni its branches, Duḥśāsana its abundant flowers and fruit, and the unwise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra is its root.
data.anv: दुर्योधनः मन्यु-मयः महा-द्रुमः, कर्णः स्कन्धः, शकुनिः तस्य शाखाः, दुःशासनः समृद्धे पुष्प-फले, अमनीषी राजा धृतराष्ट्रः मूलम् ॥

data.v: युधिष्ठिरो धर्ममयो महाद्रुमः; स्कन्धोऽर्जुनो भीमसेनोऽस्य शाखाः । माद्रीसुतौ पुष्पफले समृद्धे; मूलं कृष्णो ब्रह्म च ब्राह्मणाश्च ॥
data.es: Yudhiṣṭhira is a great tree made of righteousness; Arjuna is its trunk, Bhīmasena its branches, the two sons of Mādrī its abundant flowers and fruit, and Kṛṣṇa, the Vedas, and the Brāhmaṇas are its root.
data.anv: युधिष्ठिरः धर्म-मयः महा-द्रुमः, अर्जुनः स्कन्धः, भीमसेनः अस्य शाखाः, माद्री-सुतौ समृद्धे पुष्प-फले, कृष्णः ब्रह्म च ब्राह्मणाः च मूलम् ॥

data.v: पाण्डुर्जित्वा बहून्देशान्युधा विक्रमणेन च । अरण्ये मृगयाशीलो न्यवसत्सजनस्तदा ॥
data.es: Then Pāṇḍu, having conquered many lands through battle and valor, resided in the forest with his family, devoted to the chase.
data.anv: तदा पाण्डुः युधा विक्रमणेन च बहून् देशान् जित्वा अरण्ये स-जनः मृगया-शीलः (सन्) न्यवसत् ॥

data.v: मृगव्यवायनिधने कृच्छ्रां प्राप स आपदम् । जन्मप्रभृति पार्थानां तत्राचारविधिक्रमः ॥
data.es: Due to the killing of a deer during its mating, he met with a difficult calamity; therein is described the life of the sons of Pṛthā from their birth and their progressive rites of conduct.
data.anv: मृग-व्यवाय-निधने सः कृच्छ्राम् आपदम् प्राप, तत्र पार्थानाम् जन्म-प्रभृति आचार-विधि-क्रमः (उक्तः) ॥

data.v: मात्रोरभ्युपपत्तिश्च धर्मोपनिषदं प्रति । धर्मस्य वायोः शक्रस्य देवयोश्च तथाश्विनोः ॥
data.es: It describes the approach of the two mothers towards the secret knowledge of Dharma, and the birth of the Pāṇḍavas from the deities Dharma, Vāyu, Śakra, and the two Aśvins.
data.anv: धर्म-उपनिषदम् प्रति मात्रोः अभ्युपपत्तिः च, (तथा) धर्मस्य वायोः शक्रस्य तथा अश्विनोः देवयोः (सकाशात् पार्थानाम् उत्पत्तिः उक्ता) ॥

data.v: तापसैः सह संवृद्धा मातृभ्यां परिरक्षिताः । मेध्यारण्येषु पुण्येषु महतामाश्रमेषु च ॥
data.es: Protected by their two mothers, the Pāṇḍavas grew up alongside ascetics in holy, pure forests and the hermitages of great sages.
data.anv: (ते) मातृभ्याम् परिरक्षिताः (सन्तः) तापसैः सह पुण्येषु मेध्य-अरण्येषु महताम् आश्रमेषु च संवृद्धाः (अभवन्) ।

data.v: ऋषिभिश्च तदानीता धार्तराष्ट्रान्प्रति स्वयम् । शिशवश्चाभिरूपाश्च जटिला ब्रह्मचारिणः ॥
data.es: Then, the sages personally brought them to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the children were handsome, wearing matted hair, and living as celibate students.
data.anv: तदा ऋषिभिः स्वयम् धार्तराष्ट्रान् प्रति आनीताः (ते) शिशवः च अभिरूपाः च जटिलाः ब्रह्मचारिणः (आसन्) ।

data.v: पुत्राश्च भ्रातरश्चेमे शिष्याश्च सुहृदश्च वः । पाण्डवा एत इत्युक्त्वा मुनयोऽन्तर्हितास्ततः ॥
data.es: Declaring, 'These Pāṇḍavas are your sons, brothers, students, and friends,' the sages then vanished from sight.
data.anv: एते वः पुत्राः च भ्रातरः च शिष्याः च सुहृदः च पाण्डवाः (सन्ति) इति उक्त्वा ततः मुनयः अन्तर्हिताः (अभवन्) ।

data.v: तांस्तैर्निवेदितान्दृष्ट्वा पाण्डवान्कौरवास्तदा । शिष्टाश्च वर्णाः पौरा ये ते हर्षाच्चुक्रुशुर्भृशम् ॥
data.es: Upon seeing the Pāṇḍavas thus introduced, the Kauravas, the other noble classes, and the citizens shouted loudly out of sheer joy.
data.anv: तदा तैः निवेदितान् तान् पाण्डवान् दृष्ट्वा कौरवाः ये शिष्टाः वर्णाः पौराः च (आसन्) ते हर्षात् भृशम् चुक्रुशुः ।

data.v: आहुः केचिन्न तस्यैते तस्यैत इति चापरे । यदा चिरमृतः पाण्डुः कथं तस्येति चापरे ॥
data.es: Some said, 'They are not his'; others said, 'They are his.' Some even questioned, 'Since Pāṇḍu died long ago, how can they be his?'
data.anv: केचित् आहुः एते तस्य न (सन्ति) अपरे च (आहुः) एते तस्य (सन्ति) इति अपरे च (आहुः) यदा पाण्डुः चिर-मृतः (तदा) तस्य कथम् इति ।

data.v: स्वागतं सर्वथा दिष्ट्या पाण्डोः पश्याम संततिम् । उच्यतां स्वागतमिति वाचोऽश्रूयन्त सर्वशः ॥
data.es: Voices were heard everywhere saying, 'A total welcome! By good fortune, we behold the progeny of Pāṇḍu. Let them be welcomed!'
data.anv: सर्वथा स्वागतम् दिष्ट्या पाण्डोः संततिम् पश्याम स्वागतम् इति उच्यताम् (इति) वाचः सर्वशः अश्रूयन्त ।

data.v: तस्मिन्नुपरते शब्दे दिशः सर्वा विनादयन् । अन्तर्हितानां भूतानां निस्वनस्तुमुलोऽभवत् ॥
data.es: When that noise subsided, a tumultuous sound from invisible beings arose, making all directions resonate.
data.anv: तस्मिन् शब्दे उपरते सर्वाः दिशः विनादयन् अन्तर्हितानाम् भूतानाम् तुमुलः निस्वनः तु अभवत् ।

data.v: पुष्पवृष्टिः शुभा गन्धाः शङ्खदुन्दुभिनिस्वनाः । आसन्प्रवेशे पार्थानां तदद्भुतमिवाभवत् ॥
data.es: During the entrance of the sons of Pṛthā, there was a rain of flowers, fragrant scents, and the sounding of conchs and drums; it was like a marvel.
data.anv: पार्थानाम् प्रवेशे शुभ-गन्धाः पुष्प-वृष्टिः शङ्ख-दुन्दुभि-निस्वनाः च आसन् तत् अद्भुतम् इव अभवत् ।

data.v: तत्प्रीत्या चैव सर्वेषां पौराणां हर्षसंभवः । शब्द आसीन्महांस्तत्र दिवस्पृक्कीर्तिवर्धनः ॥
data.es: Due to the affection of all the citizens, there arose a great, fame-increasing sound of joy that touched the very heavens.
data.anv: तत्र सर्वेषाम् पौराणाम् तत्-प्रीत्या च एव हर्ष-संभवः महान् कीर्ति-वर्धनः दिव-स्पृक् शब्दः आसीत् ।

data.v: तेऽप्यधीत्याखिलान्वेदाञ्शास्त्राणि विविधानि च । न्यवसन्पाण्डवास्तत्र पूजिता अकुतोभयाः ॥
data.es: Having studied all the Vedas and various scriptures, those Pāṇḍavas lived there, honored and free from fear.
data.anv: ते पाण्डवाः अपि अखिलान् वेदान् विविधानि शास्त्राणि च अधीत्य पूजिताः अकुतोभयाः (सन्तः) तत्र न्यवसन् ।

data.v: युधिष्ठिरस्य शौचेन प्रीताः प्रकृतयोऽभवन् । धृत्या च भीमसेनस्य विक्रमेणार्जुनस्य च ॥
data.es: The subjects were delighted by the purity of Yudhiṣṭhira, the fortitude of Bhīmasena, and the prowess of Arjuna.
data.anv: युधिष्ठिरस्य शौचेन भीमसेनस्य धृत्या च अर्जुनस्य विक्रमेण च प्रकृतयः प्रीताः अभवन् ।

data.v: गुरुशुश्रूषया कुन्त्या यमयोर्विनयेन च । तुतोष लोकः सकलस्तेषां शौर्यगुणेन च ॥
data.es: The entire world was pleased by Kuntī's service to elders, the humility of the twins (Nakula and Sahadeva), and the collective heroic qualities of the brothers.
data.anv: कुन्त्याः गुरु-शुश्रूषया यमयोः विनयेन च तेषां शौर्य-गुणेन च सकलः लोकः तुतोष ।

data.v: समवाये ततो राज्ञां कन्यां भर्तृस्वयंवराम् । प्राप्तवानर्जुनः कृष्णां कृत्वा कर्म सुदुष्करम् ॥
data.es: Then, in an assembly of kings, Arjuna won the maiden Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) at her svayaṃvara after performing an exceedingly difficult feat.
data.anv: ततः राज्ञां समवाये सु-दुष्करं कर्म कृत्वा अर्जुनः भर्तृ-स्वयंवराम् कन्यां कृष्णाम् प्राप्तवान् ।

data.v: ततः प्रभृति लोकेऽस्मिन्पूज्यः सर्वधनुष्मताम् । आदित्य इव दुष्प्रेक्ष्यः समरेष्वपि चाभवत् ॥
data.es: From that time on, he became worshipful among all archers in this world and, like the sun, difficult to gaze upon in battles.
data.anv: ततः प्रभृति अस्मिन् लोके (सः) सर्व-धनुष्मताम् पूज्यः समरेषु अपि आदित्यः इव दुष्प्रेक्ष्यः च अभवत् ।

data.v: स सर्वान्पार्थिवाञ्जित्वा सर्वांश्च महतो गणान् । आजहारार्जुनो राज्ञे राजसूयं महाक्रतुम् ॥
data.es: Having conquered all kings and all great tribes, Arjuna brought the great Rājasūya sacrifice to the King (Yudhiṣṭhira).
data.anv: सः अर्जुनः सर्वान् पार्थिवान् सर्वान् महतः गणान् च जित्वा राज्ञे राजसूयम् महा-क्रतुम् आजहार ।

data.v: अन्नवान्दक्षिणावांश्च सर्वैः समुदितो गुणैः । युधिष्ठिरेण संप्राप्तो राजसूयो महाक्रतुः ॥
data.es: The great Rājasūya sacrifice, abounding in food and gifts and endowed with all auspicious merits, was successfully accomplished by Yudhiṣṭhira.
